The Manual of Harmonious Rationality

A Comprehensive Moral Framework for Thinking, Acting, and Living

Constructivist Realism: Grounding Ethics in Consciousness, Coordination, and Honest Inquiry

[Author Name]

First Edition

Preface

This book tries to answer a question: how should a conscious being think and act, given what we actually know about reality?

The question is old. Every moral tradition has offered answers — religious commandments, philosophical systems, cultural customs, personal intuitions. Most of these answers get something right. None of them gets everything right. This book is an attempt to build a moral framework that gets more right than any single existing alternative, by honestly engaging with the best ideas from every tradition and absorbing what survives scrutiny.

The framework is called Constructivist Realism. Values are constructed by conscious agents — they are not handed down from above or discovered floating free in the universe. But the construction is not arbitrary. It is constrained by objective features of reality: the physics of consciousness (suffering and flourishing are real states of real systems), the mathematics of coordination (game theory describes how agents who need to cooperate actually succeed or fail), and the biology of the agent (human cognition is systematically biased in ways that moral reasoning must account for). A moral system that ignores these constraints will fail, just as a bridge designed without regard for physics will collapse.

What This Book Is

This is a comprehensive moral philosophy — foundations, decision architecture, personal ethics, political theory, economic theory, frontier problems, and defense against rival systems — developed from first principles in forty-eight chapters across nine books.

Book I establishes the foundations: why we need a new system, what epistemology demands, how value is grounded in consciousness, what evolution tells us about our moral instincts, and what we honestly do not know.

Book II diagnoses the enemy: coordination failure — the game-theoretic dynamics that produce most unnecessary suffering in the world. Morality, on this view, is the technology we invent to defeat these dynamics.

Book III builds the moral architecture: a dual-process system where pre-committed rules handle daily life and a narrow consequentialist override handles genuine crises, supported by specific virtues and a developmental trajectory from instinct through reflection to informed habit.

Books IV through VI apply the system: personal ethics (relationships, meaning, suffering, death), political philosophy (the state, institutions, rights, democracy, speech, justice, war, policy evaluation), and economic philosophy (markets, externalities, welfare, labor, fiscal policy).

Book VII confronts the frontier: existential risk, artificial intelligence, bioethics, the environment, and digital life — the places where the framework is most stretched and most needed.

Book VIII defends the system: head-to-head engagements with divine command theory, nihilism, utilitarianism, deontology, relativism, Rawlsian contractualism, virtue ethics, Marxism, and natural law — followed by a synthesis of what we take from each.

Book IX puts it all together: a complete map of the system, a reading syllabus for those who want to go deeper, and a closing oath — a set of specific commitments for those who find the arguments persuasive.

What This Book Is Not

This book is not a final word. It is explicitly designed to be revised. Every substantive claim is registered in a Position Registry with a confidence rating and a vulnerability rating. When a better position is found, the old one is swapped out and the swap is documented. The book’s architecture includes its own error-correction mechanism — not because the author expects to be wrong about everything, but because any framework that cannot update when challenged is dogma, not philosophy.

This book is not a political program. It generates positions on political and economic questions, but those positions do not map cleanly onto any existing party or ideology. Readers who expect consistent alignment with progressive, conservative, or libertarian agendas will be disappointed. The framework follows the analysis wherever it leads, which means different questions produce different conclusions.

This book is not a religion or a substitute for one. It does not require abandoning existing spiritual commitments. Its arguments are compatible with personal religious belief — many of its conclusions overlap with the moral content of the major religious traditions. What it does not accept is that moral reasoning should rest on claims whose verification depends on religious authority.

How to Read This Book

The book is designed to be read in order, since each book builds on the ones before it. But it can also be entered at different points:

  • A reader interested primarily in political philosophy can start at Book V (Chapter 17), with Book I summaries providing the necessary context.
  • A reader interested in how the framework handles rival systems can start at Book VIII (Chapter 36), using the Complete Map (Chapter 46) for orientation.
  • A reader who wants the practical takeaway can read Book IV (Chapters 13-16) and the Oath (Chapter 48), then work backward through the arguments.
  • A reader who wants the full argument should start at Chapter 1 and read straight through.

Chapter 24 (Policy Evaluation) is the hinge chapter — it develops the method by which the framework engages specific political and economic questions, and it applies to everything that follows. Readers who plan to engage with the applied chapters should read it regardless of their entry point.

A Note on Sources

The framework draws on a specific intellectual tradition — rationalist epistemology, game theory, evolutionary psychology, analytic political philosophy, Austrian and institutional economics — and engages with traditions beyond it: Kantian ethics, Rawlsian contractualism, virtue ethics, natural law theory, Confucian role ethics, Buddhist psychology, Ubuntu philosophy, the ethics of care. Every effort has been made to present rival positions in their strongest form before critiquing them. Chapter 47 (The Syllabus) provides a full reading list for those who want to verify this for themselves.

Direct quotes from primary sources appear throughout. The reader should be able to trace any major claim to its source and evaluate the argument independently.

Acknowledgments

[To be completed by the author.]

The book that follows is one answer to the question of how to live. It is offered not with the certainty that it is right, but with the confidence that it is serious, honest, comprehensive, and better than doing nothing. If the reader finds a better answer, the framework’s own principles require adopting it. That is, in the end, the strongest claim the book can make: it tells you to replace it when something better comes along.

Book I: Foundations — What Is Real?

Chapter 1: The Third Way — Why We Need a New Moral System

“The suffering of a conscious being matters.” — The Axiom

The Ruins

We are heirs to a catastrophe.

For most of human history, moral questions had a simple answer: God said so. The details varied — Yahweh, Allah, Brahma, the Tao — but the structure was universal. There existed a cosmic authority whose will defined right and wrong, and the task of the moral agent was obedience. This was the Theistic Map.

It was a powerful map. It gave billions of people a reason to cooperate, a framework for sacrifice, a vocabulary for justice, and a horizon of meaning that stretched past death. Its track record includes hospitals, universities, abolitionist movements, and the concept of universal human dignity. Anyone who dismisses it as mere superstition hasn’t studied it.

But it had a fatal flaw: its foundations were unverifiable.

The God who underwrites divine command theory cannot be tested, measured, or falsified. When two theologians disagree about God’s will — as they always do — there is no empirical procedure for settling the dispute. The map cannot be checked against the territory. And so the tradition that built cathedrals also built inquisitions, because a moral system grounded in faith has no principled mechanism for error-correction. It can only assert louder.

Then came the Enlightenment, and with it the demolition crew. Hume severed “is” from “ought”: “In every system of morality, which I have hitherto met with,” he wrote, “the author proceeds for some time in the ordinary way of reasoning… when of a sudden I am surpriz’d to find, that instead of the usual copulations of propositions, is, and is not, I meet with no proposition that is not connected with an ought, or an ought not” (A Treatise of Human Nature, III.1.1). Darwin revealed that our moral intuitions were installed by a blind process optimizing for gene replication, not truth. Nietzsche announced that God was dead — “God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him” (The Gay Science, §125) — and asked what could replace the moral framework that had depended on Him. The logical positivists argued that moral statements were literally meaningless — emotion dressed up as fact.

This was the Nihilistic Map. Or rather, the absence of a map.

Its diagnosis was correct: the theistic foundations really were unverifiable. But its prescription was disastrous. If nothing matters, then nothing prevents the strong from devouring the weak. If all values are arbitrary preferences, then there is no principled difference between a hospital and an extermination camp — only a difference in taste. The twentieth century demonstrated what happens when societies internalize this conclusion. The body count was extraordinary.

Most people today live in the rubble between these two failures. They sense that the religious answers don’t survive scrutiny, but they also sense — correctly — that nihilism is unlivable. So they improvise. They invoke “human rights” and “dignity” while quietly aware that they cannot justify these concepts from first principles. They moralize passionately on social media while lacking any coherent theory of what makes anything right or wrong.

This is not a stable equilibrium. The cracks are visible everywhere: in the collapse of institutional trust, in the retreat into tribal epistemologies, in the rise of movements that explicitly reject liberal values, in the quiet despair of people who have everything except a reason to get out of bed.

We need a new map. Not a return to the old one, and not the nihilist’s refusal to navigate at all. A third option.

The Specifications

Before building, we should be honest about what a moral system needs to do. Not what would be nice, but what is required — the minimum viable specifications for an ethical framework that can actually function in the world.

Specification 1: Grounding. The system must be built on something real — not on faith claims that can’t be tested, but also not on nothing. It needs a foundation that a rigorous skeptic can examine and, at minimum, cannot dismiss without contradiction.

Specification 2: Decision procedure. The system must actually tell you what to do. A moral framework that offers beautiful principles but no guidance when you’re standing at a genuine dilemma is philosophy as decoration. The system needs an algorithm — not in the sense of mechanical computation, but in the sense of a structured process for moving from uncertainty to action.

Specification 3: Coordination. Morality is not a single-player game. A system that produces excellent individuals who cannot cooperate with each other has failed at its most basic function. The framework must explain how agents coordinate — how trust is built, how defection is punished, how collective action problems are solved.

Specification 4: Error-correction. The system must be able to update. Any moral framework that treats its current positions as final has already started dying. The mechanism for revision must be built into the architecture, not bolted on as an afterthought.

Specification 5: Livability. The system must be something a real human being can actually follow — not a saint, not a philosopher-king, but a normally flawed person with limited willpower, imperfect information, and finite computational resources. If the system demands perfection, it will be adopted by no one and change nothing.

Specification 6: Comprehensiveness. The system must have something to say about the hard cases — not just “don’t steal,” but about war, poverty, technology, future generations, consciousness, political design, economic structure, and the dozens of other domains where moral questions actually bite. A system that only handles easy cases is a toy.

Specification 7: Competitive robustness. The system must survive contact with the strongest rival frameworks. It cannot wave away utilitarianism, dismiss Kantian ethics, or ignore the deep insights of virtue theory, contractualism, or non-Western moral traditions. It must engage them honestly, take what is true, and show where they break.

These are severe requirements. No existing system meets all of them simultaneously. Utilitarianism is strong on decision procedure but collapses under demandingness and produces repugnant conclusions about individual rights. Kantian deontology is strong on rights but cannot handle conflicts between duties and lacks empirical grounding. Virtue ethics takes character seriously but offers no decision procedure — it tells you to be virtuous without specifying what virtue requires in any concrete case. Religious ethics grounds morality in authority but fails at error-correction. Relativism abandons the project entirely.

The system we are building — which we call Constructivist Realism as a working name — aims to meet all seven specifications simultaneously. Whether it succeeds is for the reader to judge as the argument unfolds. But the ambition is explicit: we are trying to build the best available moral system, and we are willing to steal the best ideas from every tradition to do it.

The Third Way: Constructivist Realism

The name captures the essential move: values are constructed by conscious agents but constrained by objective features of reality.

Consider an analogy. Bridge-building is a human activity. There is no Platonic Form of a bridge floating in abstract space. Bridges are invented, designed, and built by people with specific goals (crossing rivers, connecting cities, carrying trains). In this sense, bridges are constructed.

But you cannot build any bridge you want. Physics constrains you. If you ignore the tensile strength of your materials, your bridge collapses. If you ignore load distribution, your bridge collapses. If you pretend gravity doesn’t exist, your bridge collapses. The laws of physics don’t design the bridge, but they ruthlessly veto bad designs. Any engineer who says “my bridge, my rules” is about to kill people.

Morality works the same way.

Moral systems are constructed by conscious agents trying to navigate the world. There is no cosmic tablet with “THOU SHALT” etched in the quantum field. In this sense, the nihilists are right: morality is not written in the atoms.

But there are objective constraints on which moral systems work and which collapse. The constraints come from three sources:

1. The physics of consciousness (valence). Suffering and joy are objective physical states of conscious systems. When a nerve fires a pain signal, something is happening in the physical world that is qualitatively different from when a nerve fires a pleasure signal. A moral system that ignores this — that treats suffering as unreal or irrelevant — is like an engineer who ignores gravity.

We develop this argument in full in Chapter 3. For now, the key claim: in a universe containing conscious minds, valence (the suffering-joy spectrum) is the objective bedrock on which any viable moral system must build. Not the only consideration — but the non-negotiable foundation.

2. The mathematics of coordination (game theory). Conscious agents who interact repeatedly face a precise mathematical landscape of cooperation and defection. Some strategies dominate others. Some equilibria are stable, others collapse. Some institutional designs produce cooperation and others produce mutual ruin.

These facts are as objective as the laws of physics. The Prisoner’s Dilemma is not a cultural construct. The Tragedy of the Commons is not a Western invention. Any group of interacting agents — human, alien, artificial — will face these same structural problems, and the viable solutions are constrained by the same mathematics. A moral system that ignores game theory is like an engineer who ignores material science: beautiful designs that cannot bear weight.

3. The biology of the agent (evolutionary psychology). The agents who must implement this moral system are not blank slates. They are products of millions of years of evolution, running on hardware optimized for gene replication in ancestral environments — with predictable biases, limited computational capacity, strong emotions, and moral intuitions installed by natural selection for purposes that have nothing to do with truth or goodness.

A moral system that assumes perfectly rational agents will fail in practice even if it succeeds in theory. A viable system must be designed for the actual hardware it runs on.

The Axiom: Where the Normativity Enters

Every logical system requires axioms — starting points that are assumed rather than proved. Euclidean geometry assumes that parallel lines never meet. Mathematics assumes that the successor function produces a new number. Physics assumes that the laws of nature are uniform across space and time.

Moral systems are no different. You cannot derive an “ought” from an “is” alone — Hume was right about that. The system requires at least one normative starting point that is chosen rather than proved.

We choose this one:

The suffering of a conscious being matters.

This is our axiom. We do not claim to prove it from purely factual premises. We claim something more modest but also more powerful: that it is the most defensible axiom available, because denying it is performatively incoherent.

Here is what we mean. Suppose someone claims: “Suffering does not matter.” Ask them: “Would you be indifferent to being tortured?” If they say yes, they are lying (and you can test this empirically). If they say no, they have just admitted that suffering matters — at least their own. And if their own suffering matters, they need a principled reason why others’ suffering doesn’t, which puts the burden of proof squarely on the denier.

This is not a logical proof. It is a demonstration that the denial cannot be sincerely held by any conscious being. When the dentist’s drill touches the nerve, postures dissolve.

Note what we are not claiming:

  • We are not claiming that all suffering is equal (it isn’t — a stubbed toe is not a genocide).
  • We are not claiming that suffering is the only thing that matters (it isn’t — autonomy, knowledge, beauty, and connection are also genuine values, which we will address in Chapter 3).
  • We are not claiming that the axiom tells you what to do in any specific case (it doesn’t — that’s what the rest of the book is for).
  • We are not claiming to have solved the is-ought problem (we haven’t — we have simply been explicit about where the normative bridge is, rather than hiding it).

What we are claiming is that this axiom is the smallest possible normative assumption needed to get a moral system off the ground, and that it is the hardest axiom to deny. If you can find a more defensible starting point, we want to hear it.

The Architecture in Preview

This book builds a complete moral system from the foundation just described. Understanding the structure now will help the reader track the argument as it develops.

Book I (Chapters 1-5): Foundations. We establish the metaphysical and epistemic bedrock. What is real? How do we know? Why does consciousness ground value? How do we deal with evolutionary instincts? What about the hard problem of consciousness and free will? These chapters must be airtight, because everything else depends on them.

Book II (Chapters 6-8): The Enemy. We diagnose why the world is full of suffering despite no one wanting it to be. The answer is coordination failure — what we call Moloch, after Allen Ginsberg’s poem. Game theory provides the formal analysis. This section is the “engine” that powers the system’s practical recommendations: morality is the technology we invent to defeat Moloch.

Book III (Chapters 9-12): The Moral Architecture. We build the decision-making system. The core innovation is dual-process ethics: default to pre-computed rules and virtues for daily life (Mode A), switch to explicit consequentialist calculation only when rule-following would produce catastrophic outcomes (Mode B). This is not a compromise between deontology and consequentialism — it is an architecture that explains when each is appropriate and why.

Book IV (Chapters 13-16): Personal Ethics. The system applied to individual life — relationships, identity, meaning, suffering, death. This is the livability test. If the system cannot help a real person navigate real life, it has failed.

Book V (Chapters 17-24): Political Philosophy. Eight full chapters of political theory derived from the foundations. Not a sidebar — a comprehensive political philosophy covering the state, institutions, rights, democracy, speech, justice, war, and policy evaluation.

Book VI (Chapters 25-30): Economic Philosophy. Six chapters of economic theory. Markets as information systems, property and exchange, externalities, the safety net, labor and automation, fiscal policy. Again, derived from the same foundations, not imported from a separate ideology.

Book VII (Chapters 31-35): The Frontier. Where the system meets problems it wasn’t designed for: existential risk, artificial intelligence, bioethics, environmental ethics, digital life. These chapters contain the most provisional positions and the most honest uncertainty.

Book VIII (Chapters 36-45): Defense. Head-to-head debates with every major rival moral system. Not dismissals — genuine engagements. Steel-man the opponent’s strongest case, then show where it breaks. The final chapter of this section is The Synthesis, where we honestly acknowledge what we took from each rival tradition.

Book IX (Chapters 46-48): Synthesis. The complete system in one view, the reading path for further study, and the commitment.

The Rules of Engagement

This book plays by rules that the reader should know upfront, because they are part of the system’s claim to intellectual honesty.

Rule 1: No sacred cows. Every position in this book is registered in a Position Registry with a confidence rating and a vulnerability rating. If a position is weak, we say so. If we find a better position during writing, we swap it in and document the change. The goal is truth, not consistency with our starting point.

Rule 2: Steel-man before attack. When we engage a rival system, we present its strongest possible version — not the version believed by its worst adherents, but the version defended by its best thinkers. If we cannot state the opposing view in a way its proponents would endorse, we have not earned the right to criticize it.

Rule 3: Show your work. Every major claim is backed by an argument, not just an assertion. If the argument is strong, it should be able to survive the reader’s skepticism. If it can’t, it should be flagged as provisional and subjected to further development.

Rule 4: Admit uncertainty. Some positions in this book are axioms — explicitly chosen starting points. Some are strong conclusions well-supported by argument. Some are provisional best guesses. We label them as such, and we mean it. A system that pretends to certainty it doesn’t have is not a system worth trusting.

Rule 5: Steal the best ideas. This system has no loyalty to any intellectual tradition. If utilitarianism has a better answer on some question, we take it. If Confucian role ethics illuminates something our Western-rationalist starting point missed, we absorb it. If Marxist structural critique identifies a real problem our framework underweights, we fix the framework. The system wins by being the most comprehensive and the most honest, not by being the most ideologically pure.

The Challenge

Here is the claim this book defends:

It is possible to build a moral system that is grounded in objective features of reality, provides actionable decision procedures, solves coordination problems, corrects its own errors, can be lived by real human beings, addresses the full range of moral questions, and survives engagement with the strongest rival frameworks.

This is an ambitious claim. It may be wrong. But the project is worth attempting, because the alternative — continuing to navigate with broken maps — has a cost measured in human suffering.

The reader’s role is not to agree, but to pressure-test. Every chapter that follows is an invitation: Find the weakness. Find the better position. If you can break this argument, you’ve improved the system. A moral framework that fears criticism is one that knows, at some level, that it deserves it.

Let us begin.

Chapter 2: The Map and the Territory — Epistemology as Moral Duty

“Being in scout mindset means wanting your ‘map’ — your perception of yourself and the world — to be as accurate as possible.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

The Moral Case for Seeing Clearly

You cannot act rightly in a world you see wrongly.

This is not a philosophical abstraction. It is a claim about the physics of action. Every decision you make rests on a model of reality — a map of the territory. If your map says the bridge can hold your weight and the territory says it cannot, you fall. If your map says the policy reduces poverty and the territory says it increases homelessness, real people suffer. If your map says the tribe across the river is subhuman and the territory says they are conscious beings with the same capacity for suffering you have, your error has moral consequences measured in blood.

The first chapter established that suffering matters. This chapter makes the connection that many moral systems leave implicit: if suffering matters, then seeing reality clearly is not an optional intellectual virtue — it is a moral obligation.

The argument is simple:

  1. Actions based on false beliefs produce worse outcomes than actions based on true beliefs (on average, over time).
  2. Worse outcomes mean more unnecessary suffering (by the valence axiom, that matters).
  3. Therefore, you have a moral duty to form accurate beliefs.

This is Epistemic Duty — the claim that truth-seeking is not merely an intellectual preference but a prerequisite for ethical action. You cannot reliably reduce suffering with a map that lies to you. And if you choose a comforting lie over a harsh truth — if you cling to a false model because it makes you feel good — then you bear moral responsibility for the damage your false model causes.

“The best description of motivated reasoning I’ve ever seen comes from psychologist Tom Gilovich. When we want something to be true, he said, we ask ourselves, ‘Can I believe this?,’ searching for an excuse to accept it. When we don’t want something to be true, we instead ask ourselves, ‘Must I believe this?,’ searching for an excuse to reject it.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

This is a description of a moral failure, not merely an intellectual one. The person who asks “Can I believe this?” about a comforting falsehood is building their decisions — and everyone affected by those decisions — on a foundation they have deliberately chosen not to inspect.

The Hardware Problem

The moral duty to see clearly would be straightforward if our minds were designed for truth. They are not.

Daniel Kahneman spent a career cataloging the ways human cognition systematically fails. His findings are devastating for anyone who assumes sincere effort is sufficient for accurate belief:

“System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary control.”

“System 2 allocates attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it, including complex computations. The operations of System 2 are often associated with the subjective experience of agency, choice, and concentration.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

The dual-process model is now one of the best-established findings in cognitive science. Your brain runs two fundamentally different systems. System 1 — fast, automatic, effortless — handles the vast majority of your cognition: recognizing faces, reading emotions, generating gut reactions. System 2 — slow, deliberate, effortful — handles complex reasoning and careful calculation.

The problem is that System 2 is lazy. It outsources most of its work to System 1, endorsing the fast system’s outputs with minimal scrutiny:

“Most of what you (your System 2) think and do originates in your System 1, but System 2 takes over when things get difficult, and it normally has the last word.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

In practice, “the last word” is often a rubber stamp. System 1 generates an answer; System 2 feels a vague sense of rightness; the answer is accepted. The subjective experience is of careful deliberation. The reality is cognitive autopilot.

And System 1 is riddled with biases — not random errors, but systematic ones that push in predictable directions:

Anchoring. Your estimate of an unknown quantity is dragged toward whatever number was recently in your environment, even if that number is obviously irrelevant. German judges with fifteen years of experience sentenced a shoplifter to significantly different prison terms depending on whether they had just rolled a 3 or a 9 on loaded dice. As Kahneman documented: “the anchoring effect was 50%.” These were not novices. They were experts, convinced they were immune. They were not.

Availability. You judge the frequency of events by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual statistics. Kahneman found that “strokes cause almost twice as many deaths as all accidents combined, but 80% of respondents judged accidental death to be more likely.” Why? Because accidents are vivid, memorable, and heavily covered by media. Strokes are not. Your System 1 substitutes “ease of recall” for “actual frequency” and never tells you it made the swap.

Representativeness. You judge probability by resemblance rather than by base rates. Kahneman’s famous “Linda problem” — where 85-90% of undergraduates judged that Linda is more likely to be “a bank teller and active in the feminist movement” than simply “a bank teller” — demonstrates a logical impossibility that System 1 produces with total confidence. A conjunction cannot be more probable than either of its components. But System 1 doesn’t do probability; it does storytelling.

WYSIATI (What You See Is All There Is). Perhaps the most fundamental bias of all:

“System 1 excels at constructing the best possible story that incorporates ideas currently activated, but it does not (cannot) allow for information it does not have.”

“Jumping to conclusions on the basis of limited evidence is so important to an understanding of intuitive thinking, and comes up so often in this book, that I will use a cumbersome abbreviation for it: WYSIATI. System 1 is radically insensitive to both the quality and the quantity of the information that gives rise to impressions and intuitions.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

WYSIATI is the master bias. It explains why you can feel so confident based on so little evidence — the story your mind constructs from the available fragments feels complete, because System 1 has no mechanism for representing what it doesn’t know. The feeling of understanding is generated by coherence, not by evidence.

This is what we are working with: a machine that anchors on irrelevant numbers, mistakes vividness for frequency, substitutes stereotypes for statistics, and constructs confident narratives from incomplete data while feeling certain it has the full picture.

And it gets worse.

The Elephant in the Brain

The biases Kahneman documented are bad enough — they are the bugs in the cognitive software. But Kevin Simler and Robin Hanson, in The Elephant in the Brain, identified something more disturbing: many of our cognitive distortions are not bugs. They are features, installed by evolution to serve strategic functions that have nothing to do with truth.

Their central thesis: the human brain is not primarily a truth-seeking device. It is a social device, optimized for navigating coalitions, managing reputation, and signaling fitness to potential allies and mates. Self-deception is not a glitch — it is a strategy. If you can deceive yourself about your own motives, you become a more convincing deceiver of others, because you display none of the tells that accompany conscious lying.

We deceive ourselves about why we give to charity (signaling, not just altruism), why we pursue education (credentialing, not just learning), why we consume art (status, not just aesthetic pleasure), and why we hold political opinions (tribal loyalty, not just policy analysis). The “rider” — conscious, verbal reasoning — is largely a press secretary, confabulating noble justifications after the fact for whatever the “elephant” of hidden, self-serving motivation has already decided.

Jonathan Haidt’s research confirms this architecture from a different angle:

“People made moral judgments quickly and emotionally. Moral reasoning was mostly just a post hoc search for reasons to justify the judgments people had already made.” — Jonathan Haidt, The Righteous Mind

“The rider evolved because it did something useful for the elephant… the rider acts as the spokesman for the elephant, even though it doesn’t necessarily know what the elephant is really thinking. The rider is skilled at fabricating post hoc explanations for whatever the elephant has just done, and it is good at finding reasons to justify whatever the elephant wants to do next.” — Jonathan Haidt, The Righteous Mind

The picture that emerges from converging lines of research is grim. Your mind is running on hardware riddled with systematic biases (Kahneman), primarily serving social and strategic functions rather than truth-seeking (Simler & Hanson), generating moral judgments from gut reactions and then rationalizing them after the fact (Haidt), and confident in its own objectivity precisely when it is most biased (Galef).

This is why epistemic duty is not a gentle suggestion — it is a moral imperative. Given what we know about how the mind works, drifting toward truth is not an option. Truth must be fought for, deliberately, against the default currents of human cognition.

The Scout and the Soldier

Julia Galef draws a distinction that crystallizes the choice facing every moral agent:

“If directionally motivated reasoning is like being a soldier fighting off threatening evidence, accuracy motivated reasoning is like being a scout forming a map of the strategic landscape. What’s beyond that next hill? Is that a bridge over the river or are my eyes deceiving me?” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

The soldier mindset treats beliefs as territory to be defended. Evidence that supports your existing beliefs is welcomed as reinforcement; evidence that threatens them is treated as enemy action to be repelled. The question is never “Is this true?” but “Can I defend my position?”

The scout mindset treats beliefs as a map to be refined. Evidence that confirms the map is useful. Evidence that contradicts the map is more useful — it reveals where the map is wrong, and a wrong map corrected is more valuable than a right map confirmed. The question is always “Is this accurate?”

“In scout mindset, there’s no such thing as a ‘threat’ to your beliefs. If you find out you were wrong about something, great — you’ve improved your map, and that can only help you.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

Why does the soldier mindset exist at all, if it produces worse maps? Because throughout most of human history, the social benefits outweighed the epistemic costs. Galef identifies six functions that self-deception serves: comfort (avoiding painful truths), self-esteem (maintaining a flattering self-image), morale (sustaining motivation through overconfidence), persuasion (convincing others by first convincing yourself), image (signaling group membership), and belonging (maintaining standing in your tribe).

These are not trivial benefits. In the ancestral environment, being right about an inconvenient fact mattered less than being aligned with your group’s consensus. The tribal outcast who was epistemically correct but socially isolated did not survive to pass on his genes.

But — and this is the crucial turn — the modern world has changed the payoff structure.

“If our instincts undervalue truth, that’s not surprising — our instincts evolved in a different world, one better suited to the soldier. Increasingly, our world is becoming one that rewards the ability to see clearly.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

In a world of global supply chains, complex institutions, nuclear weapons, artificial intelligence, climate systems, and pandemic biology, the cost of self-deception has gone up by orders of magnitude. A tribal leader whose false beliefs led his band into a bad hunting ground lost a few dozen people a season. A national leader whose false beliefs lead to bad pandemic response loses millions. A civilization whose false beliefs about climate lead to inadequate response may lose everything.

The argument for epistemic duty is not that truth has always been the optimal strategy — it hasn’t. The argument is that in the world we now inhabit, the cost of false beliefs has become catastrophic, and the old evolutionary bargain — accuracy for belonging — is no longer one any rational agent should accept.

The Method: Bayesian Updating

If epistemic duty tells you why to seek truth, Bayesian reasoning tells you how.

The core idea is simple: beliefs should be held as probabilities, not as certainties, and updated incrementally as evidence arrives.

Formally: if you believe a hypothesis H with initial probability P(H), and you observe evidence E, your updated probability should follow Bayes’ Theorem:

P(H|E) = P(E|H) × P(H) / P(E)

In plain language: your new confidence depends on (a) how confident you were before, (b) how likely the evidence would be if your belief were true, and (c) how likely the evidence would be regardless.

You do not need to carry this formula in your head. The intuition is enough: strong prior + weak evidence = small update. Weak prior + strong evidence = large update. Evidence that is equally likely whether or not your belief is true = no update at all.

Galef makes the practical version vivid:

“A scout treats their degree of certainty as a prediction of their likelihood of being right.”

“What you’re implicitly aiming for when you tag your beliefs with various confidence levels is perfect calibration. That means your ‘50% sure’ claims are in fact correct 50 percent of the time, your ‘60% sure’ claims are correct 60 percent of the time…” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

Calibration is the behavioral test of Bayesian thinking. If you say you are 90% sure about something but turn out to be right only 60% of the time, your confidence is systematically inflated. And overconfidence, as Kahneman demonstrated, is the norm:

“Clinicians who were ‘completely certain’ of the diagnosis antemortem were wrong 40% of the time.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

“An unbiased appreciation of uncertainty is a cornerstone of rationality — but it is not what people and organizations want.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

The social pressure is relentless: appear confident, have an opinion, commit to a position. The Bayesian prescription is the opposite: hold beliefs lightly, quantify uncertainty, update when evidence warrants. Galef proposes a practical diagnostic — the equivalent bet test. Instead of asking “How confident am I?”, ask “Would I bet on this at these odds?” When real stakes enter the picture, your brain switches from “press secretary mode” to “board of directors mode.”

“Being able to tell the difference between the feeling of making a claim and the feeling of actually trying to guess what’s true. Making a claim feels like your press secretary is speaking. It feels pat; neat and tidy… Trying to guess what’s true feels like being the board of directors, deciding how to bet.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

Why Bayesianism Survives Its Objections

Three objections to Bayesian epistemology are serious enough to warrant engagement.

Objection 1: Priors are subjective. Bayesian updating requires a starting probability, and different people will start with different priors. Doesn’t this make the whole enterprise subjective?

Response: Yes, priors are subjective — and this is a feature, not a bug. What matters is that Bayesian updating is self-correcting over time. Given sufficient evidence, two reasoners who start with wildly different priors will converge on the same posterior probability. Bad priors wash out. No alternative method has this convergence property.

Objection 2: Nobody actually computes Bayes’ Theorem. Real people don’t walk around with probability distributions in their heads. Isn’t this prescriptive framework impossibly demanding?

Response: You don’t need to compute the formula any more than you need to compute Newtonian mechanics to throw a ball. The point is to internalize the qualitative structure: hold beliefs as probabilities, not identities; update in the right direction; update more for stronger evidence; notice when confidence has outrun evidence. This is a learnable skill. Galef’s entire book is about people who do it naturally — not because they carry calculators, but because they’ve cultivated the habit of asking “How sure am I really?” rather than “How can I defend my position?”

Objection 3: Some beliefs shouldn’t be held probabilistically. The physicist doesn’t hold “energy is conserved” at 93% — they hold it as a framework assumption. Moral axioms work the same way. Doesn’t Bayesianism inappropriately demand that everything be probabilistic?

Response: This is correct, and important. Not all beliefs are the same kind. Axioms (like our valence axiom) are chosen, not probabilistically assessed. Framework assumptions (like the reliability of induction) are presupposed by the epistemic enterprise itself. Bayesian updating applies to empirical beliefs — beliefs about contingent facts about the world. The distinction between these categories is real, and we respect it. The system is Bayesian about the world, not about its own foundations. (We address our foundations differently — through the methods of Chapter 1: argument, coherence testing, and the performative incoherence criterion.)

The Identity Trap

There is one obstacle to epistemic duty so powerful that it deserves its own section: the fusion of beliefs with identity.

“The problem with identity is that it wrecks your ability to think clearly. Identifying with a belief makes you feel like you have to be ready to defend it, which motivates you to focus your attention on collecting evidence in its favor.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

When a belief becomes part of who you are, updating it is no longer an intellectual operation — it is an act of self-destruction. “I am a libertarian” is not a description of a probability distribution over policy questions; it is a declaration of tribal membership, personal history, and social bonds. Changing that belief means changing your identity, your social circle, and your story about yourself. The epistemic cost of updating is compounded by an existential cost that makes the soldier mindset nearly irresistible.

Galef identifies the telltale signs: using the phrase “I believe” (turning a claim about the world into a claim about yourself), getting emotionally triggered when the belief is challenged, using defiant language (“I’m proud to say…”), gatekeeping (“You can’t call yourself an X if you believe Y”), and feeling schadenfreude when the opposing tribe suffers a setback.

Galef’s proposed solution is elegant:

“Holding an identity lightly means thinking of it in a matter-of-fact way, rather than as a central source of pride and meaning in your life. It’s a description, not a flag to be waved proudly.”

“Holding an identity lightly means treating that identity as contingent, saying to yourself, ‘I’m a liberal, for as long as it continues to seem to me that liberalism is just.’” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

This is not nihilism about identity. It is intellectual maturity. You can have convictions — strong ones, passionately held — without fusing them to your sense of self. The test is simple: can you specify what evidence would change your mind? If the answer is “nothing,” you don’t hold a belief — you hold a creed. And creeds, whatever their social utility, are epistemic death.

The lesson for our system is architectural. This book maintains a Position Registry with explicit confidence ratings and vulnerability assessments precisely to prevent the identity trap at the level of the system itself. If “our framework says X” becomes a statement of tribal loyalty rather than a revisable claim, the system has succumbed to the very disease it diagnoses. The swap mechanism is the institutional antibody against this failure.

The Twelve Epistemic Virtues

The Framework lists twelve virtues of rationality. Here we ground them in the argument of this chapter and organize them as the character traits required to fulfill epistemic duty.

The Scout Virtues (habits that make truth-seeking possible):

  1. Curiosity — the active drive to destroy your own ignorance, not merely to confirm what you already believe. The curious person asks “What am I missing?” before asking “Am I right?”

  2. Relinquishment — the ability to say “I was wrong” without ego collapse. Galef documents the case of an Oxford professor who, upon hearing evidence that his life’s work was mistaken, walked to the front of the lecture hall and said: “My dear fellow, I wish to thank you. I have been wrong these fifteen years.” This is relinquishment — and it is rare, because it requires decoupling belief from identity.

  3. Lightness — holding beliefs as probabilities, not possessions. The light thinker feels no attachment to any specific conclusion; they feel attachment to the process that produces accurate conclusions.

  4. Evenness — attacking your own arguments as ruthlessly as your opponent’s. The even thinker applies Galef’s “selective skeptic test”: if you find a study that supports your view, ask “Would I have scrutinized this study harder if it had found the opposite?” If yes, you are not even.

  5. Steel-Manning — the commitment to engage the strongest version of opposing views. Galef describes Bryan Caplan’s “Ideological Turing Test”: can you state the opposing position well enough that its proponents cannot tell you’re a critic? If you can’t pass this test, you don’t yet understand what you’re arguing against.

  6. Empiricism — the insistence that disputes about the world be settled by evidence about the world, not by authority, tradition, or rhetorical force. When the map disagrees with the ground, the map is wrong.

  7. Simplicity — Occam’s Razor applied as a Bayesian principle. Simpler hypotheses have higher prior probabilities because there are fewer ways for them to be true by coincidence. Do not multiply entities beyond necessity.

  8. Humility — the constant awareness that you are running on biased hardware. The humble thinker does not trust their first impression; they treat it as data — useful, but not authoritative.

The Soldier-Proofing Virtues (habits that protect against motivated reasoning):

  1. Precision — the practice of replacing vague, emotionally loaded words with specific, testable claims. “The economy is bad” becomes “Unemployment is at 7.2%, up from 5.1% a year ago.” Precision disarms soldier mindset by removing the tribal signals that trigger defensive reasoning.

  2. The Void — the capacity to suspend judgment when the evidence is insufficient. The untrained mind abhors uncertainty and rushes to fill it with a confident narrative (WYSIATI). The void is the discipline of sitting with “I don’t know” until knowing becomes possible.

  3. Scholarship — the duty to engage with the existing literature before forming opinions. Most of what you think is original has already been thought by someone smarter, and most of what you think is true has already been tested by someone more rigorous. Humility requires scholarship; scholarship enables genuine originality.

  4. Perfectionism (Tsuyoku Naritai — “I want to become stronger”) — the refusal to settle for “good enough” in the pursuit of understanding. This is not perfectionism about outcomes — it is perfectionism about process. The epistemic agent who coasts is the epistemic agent who drifts.

The Planning Fallacy and Moral Decision-Making

One cognitive bias deserves special attention because it has direct moral implications: the planning fallacy.

Kahneman discovered it in his own life. His team was developing a curriculum and asked a member — an experienced education expert — to estimate how long similar projects typically took. The answer: seven to ten years, with 40% of comparable teams never finishing at all. The team’s own estimate for their project? Two and a half years. They took eight.

“When forecasting the outcomes of risky projects, executives too easily fall victim to the planning fallacy. In its grip, they make decisions based on delusional optimism rather than on a rational weighting of gains, losses, and probabilities. They overestimate benefits and underestimate costs. They spin scenarios of success while overlooking the potential for mistakes and miscalculations.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

The planning fallacy is not just a project-management nuisance. It is a moral hazard. When governments underestimate the cost of a war, real people die in the gap between prediction and reality. When policymakers overestimate the effectiveness of an intervention, resources are wasted that could have reduced suffering elsewhere. When entrepreneurs overestimate their chances of success — and Kahneman found that “fully 81% of entrepreneurs put their personal odds of success at 7 out of 10 or higher” while the base rate is closer to 35% — they make decisions that affect employees, investors, and families based on delusion.

Kahneman’s remedy is the outside view: instead of asking “What is my estimate of this specific project?” ask “What typically happens to projects like this?” The outside view forces you to consult base rates — the statistical reality of how similar endeavors have actually performed — rather than constructing a flattering narrative from the inside.

This is Bayesian reasoning applied to planning. Your inside-view narrative is the prior. The base rate is the evidence. The update should move you sharply toward the base rate, because the evidence of history outweighs the coherence of your personal story.

Gary Klein proposed a complementary technique — the premortem:

“Imagine that we are a year into the future. We implemented the plan as it now exists. The outcome was a disaster. Please take 5 to 10 minutes to write a brief history of that disaster.” — Daniel Kahneman, reporting Gary Klein’s method, Thinking, Fast and Slow

The premortem works because it gives System 1 permission to search for threats instead of constructing a success narrative. It is a hack for broken hardware — a way to redirect the storytelling engine toward useful pessimism.

What Epistemic Duty Does Not Require

Epistemic duty is demanding, but it is not totalizing. Three common misunderstandings should be addressed.

It does not require emotionlessness. Emotions are data. As Kahneman’s colleague Antonio Damasio demonstrated with patients who had damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, reasoning without emotional input produces catastrophically bad decisions. Haidt’s research confirms: “Emotions are a kind of information processing. Contrasting emotion with cognition is therefore as pointless as contrasting rain with weather.” The duty is not to suppress emotion but to recognize it as input — useful, important, but not infallible.

It does not require truth-telling in all circumstances. The duty is to seek truth, not to weaponize it. Whether and how to communicate a truth is a separate moral question, governed by the dual-process architecture we develop in Chapters 9 and 10. The duty is against self-deception — against lying to yourself — not against tact, discretion, or strategic silence.

It does not require certainty before action. The world will not pause while you gather more evidence. Epistemic duty requires you to act on your best available model while remaining open to updating it. The scout does not sit in their tent until the map is perfect; they venture out with the best map they have, alert to every sign that the map is wrong.

The Epistemic Foundation

Let us take stock of what this chapter has established.

We live inside minds that were built for social survival, not for truth. Our System 1 is fast but biased. Our System 2 is capable but lazy. Our reasoning is often post hoc rationalization. Our beliefs are infected by identity, tribalism, overconfidence, and motivated reasoning.

And yet truth matters, because actions based on false beliefs produce unnecessary suffering. This gives us the moral duty to fight the default currents of our own cognition — to cultivate the scout mindset, to hold beliefs as probabilities rather than identities, to update on evidence, and to build institutions that systematize error-correction.

The method is Bayesian: hold beliefs with calibrated confidence, update when evidence warrants, and never let the coherence of your narrative substitute for the quality of your evidence.

“We talk about our beliefs as if they’re military positions, or even fortresses, built to resist attack. Beliefs can be deep-rooted, well-grounded, built on fact, and backed up by arguments… And if we do change our minds? That’s surrender.” — Julia Galef, The Scout Mindset

This book proposes a different metaphor. Your beliefs are not a fortress. They are a map. And a map that cannot be updated is not a strength — it is a liability. The scout who discovers their map is wrong has gained something. The soldier who defends a wrong map to the death has lost everything.

“The illusion that one has understood the past feeds the further illusion that one can predict and control the future. These illusions are comforting. They reduce the anxiety that we would experience if we allowed ourselves to fully acknowledge the uncertainties of existence.” — Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

Comfort is not our goal. Accuracy is. Not because accuracy feels good — often it doesn’t — but because it is the prerequisite for acting well in a world where actions have consequences measured in human suffering.

This is the epistemological foundation. We know why truth matters (it prevents suffering). We know how to pursue it (Bayesian updating, calibrated confidence, scout mindset). We know what stands in our way (biases, motivated reasoning, identity fusion). And we know what character traits the obstacles demand (the twelve epistemic virtues).

With this foundation laid, we turn to the question of origins: given that our minds were shaped by evolution, how do we decide which inherited instincts to keep and which to discard?

Chapter 3: The Axiom of Valence — Grounding Value in Consciousness

“The evolution of the capacity to simulate seems to have culminated in subjective consciousness. Why this should have happened is, to me, the most profound mystery facing modern biology.” — Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene

The Problem We Must Solve

In Chapter 1, we made a claim and a confession.

The claim: the suffering of a conscious being matters. The confession: this is an axiom — a starting point chosen rather than proved. We argued that denying it is performatively incoherent, but we left the heavy lifting for later.

This is later.

This chapter must do what no other chapter in the book can do for it: explain why valence — the spectrum from suffering to joy — provides a legitimate foundation for a moral system. Not assert it. Not appeal to intuition. Actually argue for it in a way that survives the most sophisticated objections.

The stakes are total. If this chapter fails, the rest of the book is a castle built on sand. Every political recommendation, every economic analysis, every debate with a rival system bottoms out here. If this claim cannot bear the weight, nothing above it stands.

Three specific challenges must be met:

  1. The Is-Ought Gap (Hume’s Guillotine): You cannot derive a moral obligation from a factual observation. How does the fact that suffering exists generate the obligation to reduce it?

  2. The Error Theory Challenge (Mackie): Perhaps suffering is real but moral facts are not. People act as if suffering matters, but there are no objective moral properties in the world — just subjective reactions we mistakenly project onto reality.

  3. The Scope Problem: If valence grounds morality, whose valence counts? Animals? Future AIs? Ecosystems? Where is the line, and what justifies it?

We take them in order.

What Valence Is

Before arguing that valence matters, we need to be precise about what it is.

Valence is not an emotion. It is not happiness. It is not preference satisfaction. It is the qualitative character of conscious experience along the suffering-to-flourishing spectrum — the raw fact that some states of consciousness are experienced as bad and others as good, prior to any interpretation or judgment.

Consider pain. When your hand touches a hot stove, a cascade of physical events occurs: nociceptors fire, signals travel along C-fibers and A-delta fibers to the spinal cord, the thalamus routes the information, the somatosensory cortex processes it. But something else happens too — something that constitutes what Dawkins called “the most profound mystery facing modern biology.” There is something it is like to be in pain. The neural activity doesn’t just process information; it hurts.

This “something it is like” — what philosophers call phenomenal consciousness or qualia — is the foundation we are building on. Not the neural correlates visible on brain scans, but the experience itself, known only from the inside.

Daniel Kahneman drew a crucial distinction between two aspects of wellbeing. The “experiencing self” lives in the continuous present — the you who actually feels pleasure and pain, moment to moment. The “remembering self” constructs narratives about the past and often gets the evaluation wrong. A colonoscopy patient whose procedure ended with a mild final phase rated the overall experience as less painful than one whose procedure was shorter but ended abruptly — even though the first patient experienced more total pain. The remembering self was tricked by the “peak-end rule.” The experiencing self was not.

This distinction matters because our axiom is grounded in the experiencing self, not the remembering self. What matters morally is not how people evaluate their lives in retrospect — evaluations are subject to framing effects, cognitive biases, and narrative distortions. What matters is the moment-to-moment stream of actual experience.

This is a substantive commitment, and it puts us at odds with certain versions of utilitarianism that define welfare in terms of preference satisfaction or life-satisfaction reports. We are claiming something stronger: that there is a fact of the matter about how a conscious being is doing at any given moment, and that this fact is not determined by what the being says or thinks about how it is doing, but by the actual qualitative character of its experience.

The Argument from Undeniability

We begin with the weakest-seeming but actually strongest argument for valence as a moral foundation: you cannot sincerely deny it.

Consider the following thought experiment. A philosopher publishes a paper arguing that suffering has no moral significance — that it is merely a physical state with no normative implications, like the temperature of a rock. The paper is clever, well-argued, and logically valid.

Now imagine that same philosopher strapped to a chair while someone slowly increases the electric current running through their body. At some point — early, we suspect — they will scream. They will beg for it to stop. They will offer anything to make it end.

In that moment, what has happened to their thesis?

It has not been refuted in the strict logical sense. But it cannot be acted on. The screaming, the begging, the desperate search for escape — the philosopher’s entire behavioral repertoire constitutes a living demonstration that they treat suffering as mattering.

This is performative incoherence. The denial of valence’s moral significance cannot be sincerely lived. It can only be asserted from the safety of an armchair, where the stakes are zero.

“Be warned that if you wish, as I do, to build a society in which individuals cooperate generously and unselfishly towards a common good, you can expect little help from biological nature. Let us try to teach generosity and altruism, because we are born selfish. Let us understand what our own selfish genes are up to, because we may then at least have the chance to upset their designs, something that no other species has ever aspired to.” — Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene

Dawkins is right that evolution gives us no help with morality — but notice what he takes for granted. He assumes, without arguing for it, that building “a society in which individuals cooperate generously” is a goal worth pursuing. Why? Because the alternative — a society of ruthless selfishness — would be, as he puts it elsewhere, “a very nasty society in which to live.” And “nasty” is a valence judgment. Even the arch-gene-selectionist, when he steps back from description to prescription, cannot avoid grounding his moral vision in the fact that some states of being are experienced as worse than others.

The asymmetry of denial. Notice a crucial asymmetry. The claim “suffering matters” can be lived. People routinely organize their entire lives around reducing suffering — their own and others’. The claim “suffering does not matter” cannot be lived by any conscious being. This asymmetry is not proof, but it is powerful evidence. When one side of a philosophical debate can be lived and the other cannot, we have strong reason to suspect that the livable side is tracking something real.

Crossing the Is-Ought Gap

Now for Hume’s Guillotine, the objection that most threatens us.

David Hume observed in 1739 that many moral arguments commit a subtle fallacy: they begin with statements about what is the case and suddenly switch to statements about what ought to be the case, with no justification for the leap. You cannot derive an obligation from a description. From “suffering exists” alone, you cannot conclude “suffering ought to be reduced.”

Hume was right. And we are not going to pretend otherwise.

Our system does not derive “ought” from “is.” It starts with an irreducible normative commitment — the axiom that conscious suffering matters — and then uses empirical facts to determine the best strategies for honoring that commitment. The “is” does not generate the “ought.” The “ought” is the axiom. The “is” tells us how to act on it.

This is structurally identical to how every other rational enterprise works. Engineering does not derive “bridges ought to stand up” from physics. It starts with the commitment that bridges should stand up and uses physics to determine how. Medicine does not derive “patients ought to survive” from biology. It starts with the commitment to patient welfare and uses biological knowledge to advance it. The Hippocratic Oath is not a theorem of biochemistry — it is an axiom of the medical profession.

Our system works the same way:

  • Axiom (normative): Conscious suffering matters; other things being equal, it should be reduced.
  • Empirical input: Game theory, evolutionary psychology, neuroscience, and institutional analysis tell us what actually reduces suffering in practice.
  • Output: Specific moral, political, and economic recommendations.

The is-ought gap is real, but it is not a problem for us, because we never claimed to cross it through pure logic. We claimed to locate it precisely — at the axiom — and then build rigorously on both sides. Every system needs at least one axiom. We are honest about ours.

But why this axiom? A fair objection: you can start with any axiom. Why not “the will of God matters” or “racial purity matters” or “the number of paperclips in the universe matters”?

Because not all axioms are equal. An axiom should be:

  1. Hard to deny. Our axiom passes the undeniability test above. “The will of God matters” does not — a sincere atheist can deny it without performative incoherence. “Racial purity matters” does not — members of the “inferior” race can deny it while living consistently. Only valence has the property that every conscious being, when pressed, reveals through their behavior that they treat it as mattering.

  2. Minimal. Our axiom assumes as little as possible. We don’t start with “happiness should be maximized” (that would smuggle in utilitarianism) or “persons have inherent dignity” (that would smuggle in Kantianism). We start with the bare claim that the suffering-joy spectrum is morally significant. Everything else is argued for, not assumed.

  3. Productive. Our axiom generates a rich moral system when combined with empirical knowledge. Not all axioms do. “Everything is permitted” is hard to deny from a nihilist’s perspective, but it generates nothing — it is an axiom for paralysis.

Answering the Error Theorist

J.L. Mackie, in Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977), mounted the most sophisticated attack on moral realism. His argument from “queerness” goes like this: if moral facts existed, they would be utterly unlike any other kind of fact in the universe. They would have to be simultaneously descriptive (telling us how the world is) and prescriptive (telling us what to do) — a combination found nowhere else in nature. Since such queer entities probably don’t exist, moral realism is probably false.

Mackie’s argument is serious and deserves a serious answer. Here is ours:

Valence is not “queer” in Mackie’s sense. Mackie imagined moral facts as free-floating normative properties — as if “wrongness” were an invisible substance hovering over acts of cruelty. But valence is not that kind of thing.

Valence is a physical property of conscious systems. When a person experiences agony, their brain is in a state that is detectable, measurable, and as physical as the temperature of a star. Valence is not hovering over reality; it is reality — a specific, empirically accessible subset of it.

The normative dimension enters not because valence intrinsically commands, but because it intrinsically motivates. No conscious being experiencing severe suffering needs a philosophical argument to want it to stop. The motivation is built into the experience itself. Mackie assumed that moral facts would need some mysterious power to compel action. But valence compels action the same way hunger compels eating — through the ordinary causal mechanisms of conscious experience.

The error theorist’s dilemma. Mackie claimed that when people make moral judgments, they are systematically in error — projecting subjective reactions onto the world as if they were objective facts. But consider what this means in practice. The error theorist must say: “When the torture victim screams ‘This is bad!’ they are making a factual error. Torture is not really bad — it merely causes a physical state that the victim mistakenly interprets as having normative significance.”

This is not a refutation. It is a reductio. Any philosophical position that requires you to say “torture is not really bad” has, by any sane accounting, proven too much. The error theorist has not discovered a deep truth about the nature of morality — they have demonstrated the inadequacy of their theory by showing that it conflicts with the most basic deliverance of conscious experience.

We are not claiming this settles the debate in academic metaethics; error theory remains a live position defended by serious philosophers. What we are claiming is that for practical purposes — for building a moral system that real people can use — error theory is a non-starter. A moral system cannot be built on the premise that morality is an error.

The illusionist challenge. A deeper version of the error theory comes from illusionism about consciousness (Dennett, Frankish). On this view, phenomenal consciousness — the “what it is like” that grounds our valence realism — is itself an illusion. If illusionism is correct, the physical property we are calling “valence” does not exist in the way we claim.

The framework’s response is twofold. First, illusionism faces its own reductio: “Your experience of reading this sentence is an illusion” cannot be asserted without presupposing the very phenomenon it denies. Dennett himself does not claim that pain is unreal; he claims it is differently constituted than folk psychology supposes. Second, the framework can operate on functional valence — the causally efficacious states that make beings avoid damage and seek flourishing — even if the metaphysics of phenomenal consciousness turns out differently than we assume. The axiom requires that suffering matters, not that it has a specific metaphysical character. If illusionism is true, the functional states still exist, still cause harm, and still demand moral attention.

This is an honest concession: the framework’s grounding is robust to the hard problem but not immune to it. If someone were to show that nothing even functionally analogous to suffering exists, the foundation would crack. We do not believe this is possible, but we name the dependency explicitly. Chapter 5 develops this further.

Value Beyond Suffering: The Complex Vector

A common misunderstanding must now be addressed. If valence is the foundation, does that mean we are just utilitarians in disguise — that everything reduces to maximizing pleasure and minimizing pain?

No. And the distinction is critical.

Classical utilitarianism treats value as a scalar — a single number on a pleasure-pain axis that can be summed across people and maximized. This is what Bentham meant by “the greatest happiness of the greatest number.” It is what leads to the repugnant conclusion (a world of ten billion people barely worth living is “better” than a world of one billion people flourishing) and the utility monster (a being that experiences superhuman pleasure can consume everyone else’s resources).

We treat value as a complex vector — a multi-dimensional space of qualitatively distinct goods, of which the suffering-joy axis is the foundation but not the totality.

What are the other dimensions? Drawing on the best available psychology, neuroscience, and philosophical reflection, we propose (provisionally) these irreducible components of human flourishing:

1. Hedonic tone — the suffering-to-joy axis. The foundation. A life of unrelieved agony is bad regardless of what else it contains.

2. Autonomy — the experience of being the author of one’s own actions. A life of pleasure that was entirely manipulated or controlled would be missing something essential, even if the moment-to-moment hedonic tone was positive. This is why Nozick’s Experience Machine is unsatisfying — most people would not choose a lifetime of simulated bliss over a real life with real challenges.

3. Competence — the experience of mastery and growth. Humans are not designed for static contentment. We need challenge, skill development, and the satisfaction of overcoming obstacles. This is what Csikszentmihalyi documented as “flow” — the state where challenge and skill are perfectly matched.

4. Connection — the experience of genuine relationship with other conscious beings. Solitary pleasure is not the same as shared joy. The deepest forms of human wellbeing — love, friendship, community — are inherently relational.

5. Understanding — the experience of comprehending reality. Curiosity is not a means to pleasure; it is a distinct form of flourishing. The scientist who understands a phenomenon is not merely “pleased” — they are engaging in a qualitatively different kind of good.

6. Meaning — the experience of one’s actions and existence as significant. Viktor Frankl, writing from inside Auschwitz, observed that prisoners who maintained a sense of purpose survived at higher rates than those who lost it, even when their material conditions were identical. Meaning is not reducible to hedonic tone — it is a distinct dimension of the value vector.

This list is provisional. We hold it with moderate confidence and expect it to be refined as the system develops. What we hold with high confidence is the structure: value is a vector, not a scalar. This single move dissolves most of the classic objections to welfare-based ethics:

  • The Experience Machine fails against a vector because it only provides hedonic tone while destroying autonomy, genuine connection, and real understanding.
  • The Repugnant Conclusion fails against a vector because lives “barely worth living” score near zero on most dimensions, not just hedonic tone.
  • The Utility Monster fails against a vector because you cannot aggregate qualitatively distinct goods into a single sum to be maximized.

The Evolutionary Grounding

“One way for genes to solve the problem of making predictions in rather unpredictable environments is to build in a capacity for learning. Here the program may take the form of the following instructions to the survival machine: ‘Here is a list of things defined as rewarding: sweet taste in the mouth, orgasm, mild temperature, smiling child. And here is a list of nasty things: various sorts of pain, nausea, empty stomach, screaming child.’” — Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene

Dawkins here describes something essential: valence is the mechanism by which genes steer organisms. Pain and pleasure are not accidents of biology — they are the control system. The gene cannot directly tell the organism what to do in every situation, so it installs a reward-punishment architecture and lets the organism learn.

But here is the insight that makes our moral system possible: the control system has become more important than the controller.

The gene “wants” (metaphorically) nothing more than its own replication. It uses pleasure and pain as instruments toward that end. But from the organism’s perspective — from the perspective of the conscious being who actually experiences the pleasure and pain — the valence is not a means to anything. It is the most immediate reality there is. The gene uses sugar-pleasure to make you eat calories. But you don’t experience “a gene-replication-promoting state.” You experience sweetness. The experience is real even though the gene’s “purpose” in creating it was purely instrumental.

“Whatever the philosophical problems raised by consciousness, for the purpose of this story it can be thought of as the culmination of an evolutionary trend towards the emancipation of survival machines as executive decision-takers from their ultimate masters, the genes. Not only are brains in charge of the day-to-day running of survival-machine affairs, they have also acquired the ability to predict the future and act accordingly. They even have the power to rebel against the dictates of the genes, for instance in refusing to have as many children as they are able to.” — Richard Dawkins, The Selfish Gene

This is the emancipation thesis, and it is crucial for our project. Once consciousness evolves — once there is something it is like to be an organism — the organism’s welfare becomes a fact about the world that is independent of gene-level fitness. The gene created the pain system to promote survival. But the pain is real to the organism regardless of whether it promotes survival. A person dying of cancer is in agony; the agony has no survival function; but it is absolutely real. Their suffering does not stop being a fact just because evolution has no further use for them.

This gives us a clean answer to the evolutionary debunker — the philosopher who argues that because our moral intuitions were shaped by natural selection, they are unreliable guides to moral truth. We agree that moral intuitions are unreliable. That is why we don’t ground our system in intuitions. We ground it in valence itself — the raw physical reality of conscious experience — and use reason, game theory, and empirical evidence to determine what to do about it.

Jonathan Haidt’s research demonstrates exactly how unreliable moral intuitions are:

“People made moral judgments quickly and emotionally. Moral reasoning was mostly just a post hoc search for reasons to justify the judgments people had already made.” — Jonathan Haidt, The Righteous Mind

“The mind is divided, like a rider on an elephant, and the rider’s job is to serve the elephant. The rider is our conscious reasoning — the stream of words and images of which we are fully aware. The elephant is the other 99 percent of mental processes — the ones that occur outside of awareness but that actually govern most of our behavior.” — Jonathan Haidt, The Righteous Mind

The elephant — our automatic moral intuitions — was shaped by evolution for genetic fitness, not for tracking moral truth. The rider — our conscious reasoning — is mostly a press secretary confabulating justifications after the fact. This is exactly why we cannot build a moral system on intuitions alone. Intuitions are data, but they are not foundations.

Valence is the foundation. The elephant’s reactions are variable, culturally shaped, and often biased. But the fact that there is an elephant at all — that conscious beings have experiences ranging from agony to ecstasy — is not variable. It is the common substrate beneath every moral intuition, every cultural variation, every philosophical tradition. Every moral system in human history has been built in response to the same underlying reality: conscious beings can suffer, and that suffering presses upon us with a force that demands response.

The Scope Question: Whose Valence Counts?

If valence is the moral foundation, then any system that has valence is a moral patient — an entity whose welfare must be considered. This follows directly and cannot be avoided. But it raises a hard question: which systems have valence?

We need to be honest: we do not have a complete answer. The “hard problem” of consciousness — explaining why and how physical processes give rise to subjective experience — remains unsolved. We cannot yet say with certainty which systems are conscious and which are merely processing information without any accompanying experience.

But we can say more than “we don’t know.” We can establish principles for acting under uncertainty.
