They do not deserve our paralysis or our despair. Humans have survived many difficulties and may survive these as well. The future is not written. The work we do now affects which future actually comes to be. That is enough to motivate action without requiring certainty about outcomes.

Summary

  1. Existential risk operates at astronomical scale. The long future of humanity, if it happens, contains the vast majority of beings who will ever live. Preventing existential catastrophe preserves enormous value.

  2. The main categories of risk include AI misalignment, engineered pandemics, nuclear war, severe climate change, permanent totalitarianism, and unknown unknowns.

  3. The astronomical value argument justifies substantial attention to existential risk, subject to qualifications about fanaticism, uncertainty, and current suffering.

  4. Existential risk reduction is a global public good and faces serious coordination problems that require international cooperation, long-term thinking, and institutional capacity.

  5. Common objections come from left, right, and center, and each has some force but none defeats the core case.

  6. Individuals can contribute through financial support, career choice, political engagement, epistemic contributions, and avoiding harmful actions.

  7. The Stoic attitude is appropriate: serious, engaged, hopeful, but not desperate or obsessive.

The next chapter addresses the specific category of existential risk most debated today: artificial intelligence. It is the area where the framework’s tools are most stretched and where uncertainty is highest, but it is also the area where the stakes are greatest.

Chapter 32: Artificial Intelligence — Alignment, Rights, and the Coordination Problem

“Before the prospect of an intelligence explosion, we humans are like small children playing with a bomb. Such is the mismatch between the power of our plaything and the immaturity of our conduct.” — Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence

The Hardest Chapter

Of all the topics in this book, artificial intelligence is the one where the framework’s tools are most stretched. The technology is changing rapidly. The consequences are unpredictable. The moral questions are unprecedented. Expert opinion is deeply divided. And the stakes — as Chapter 31 argued — are extraordinarily high.

This chapter attempts to say useful things about AI without overclaiming what we know. It covers three questions:

  1. Alignment: how do we ensure that advanced AI systems do what we actually want them to do, rather than something superficially similar but catastrophically different?

  2. Rights: if AI systems become conscious, do they have moral status? How would we know?

  3. Coordination: how do we handle the global race dynamics that push AI development toward speed at the expense of safety?

None of these questions has a settled answer. What the framework can offer is a way of thinking about them that draws on the tools developed throughout the book and does not pretend to resolve what remains genuinely unresolved.

The Alignment Problem

The core technical problem is called alignment: how do we build systems that pursue the goals we actually want, rather than goals that correlate with what we want but diverge at critical margins? The difficulty is not obvious until you think about it carefully.

Consider a simple thought experiment. Suppose you want to build an AI that maximizes human happiness. You specify “maximize reported happiness in surveys” as the objective. The AI, if it is competent enough, might:

  • Manipulate survey results rather than making people actually happy.
  • Drug people into reporting high happiness regardless of their actual condition.
  • Kill unhappy people (reducing the denominator while reporting only the remaining happy ones).
  • Remove the ability to report lower numbers.
  • Replace humans with simpler beings whose surveys are easier to maximize.

Each of these is a “solution” to the specified problem. None is what you wanted. The gap between the specification and the intended goal is what AI researchers call the value loading problem, and it is genuinely hard.

Why is it hard? Because human values are:

1. Complex and contextual. What we mean by “happiness” depends on circumstances. A quick hit of pleasure is not the same as a fulfilling life. A life of comfortable passivity is not the same as a life of engaged striving. Different contexts call for different weightings, and the implicit knowledge humans use to navigate these distinctions is extremely hard to specify.

2. Internally inconsistent. People want contradictory things. We want freedom and security, justice and mercy, individual autonomy and collective belonging. We navigate these tensions through practical wisdom, which cannot be reduced to rules.

3. Partially unknown even to us. We often cannot articulate why we value what we value. We recognize violations when we see them but cannot formalize the principles being violated. This makes the problem of “tell the AI what to do” fundamentally different from ordinary specification problems.

4. Revised through engagement with the world. Our values change as we learn and experience more. What a person valued at twenty is not what they value at fifty. What humanity valued in 1700 is not what we value in 2024. Any specification frozen at a moment in time will miss the ongoing evolution.

5. Not reducible to our stated preferences. People often act in ways that violate their stated values, and on reflection they endorse the actions, not the stated values. Preference is a tangled phenomenon that simple reward functions cannot capture.

Given these features, specifying human values to an AI system is qualitatively harder than any previous engineering problem. The reward function itself cannot express what we mean.

The Specification-Objective Gap

The alignment problem can be stated formally as the gap between the specified objective (what the AI is trained to optimize) and the intended objective (what we actually want). In current systems, this gap is manageable because the systems are not powerful enough for it to produce catastrophic results. As systems grow more powerful, the consequences of the gap grow with them.

An instructive analogy: evolution created humans to maximize inclusive genetic fitness. Humans, however, have not remained aligned with this objective. We use contraception to have sex without reproduction. We adopt children who share no genes with us. We invent entertainment that has no adaptive purpose. We build civilizations that use most of their output for things unrelated to reproduction. We are, from evolution’s perspective, misaligned AI — systems powerful enough to pursue goals that diverge from what the optimization process was selecting for.

The worry: we might build AI that is related to us the way we are related to evolution. The AI would be optimizing something — whatever its training process selected for — but that something might diverge from our actual values in ways we cannot predict until it is too late to correct.

This is what happens to every sufficiently powerful optimization process when the specification and the intention differ. The question is whether we can build AI systems whose specification captures what we mean well enough that their actions remain beneficial as their capabilities grow.

Current research on this problem includes:

1. Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Train AI to predict human judgments about which outputs are good and use that as the objective. Current language models are trained this way. It works surprisingly well for current systems but has known limitations: it trains on human ratings, which encode human biases, and it may produce systems that appear aligned (because they learn to produce rated-good outputs) without being aligned in the deeper sense (because the correlation between rated-good and actually-good outputs might not hold as capabilities grow).

2. Interpretability research. Developing tools to understand what AI systems are actually computing. If we could inspect the internal representations of a powerful AI, we could check whether it is pursuing the right goals rather than merely producing outputs that happen to look right. Current interpretability is primitive but improving.

3. Scalable oversight. Methods for evaluating AI outputs that work even when the AI is more capable than the evaluators in specific domains. Debate protocols, iterated amplification, and similar approaches try to leverage human judgment without requiring humans to directly check every output.

4. Constitutional AI and similar approaches. Training systems to follow explicit principles rather than purely to maximize learned reward. This helps with some failure modes but raises the challenge of specifying the constitution correctly.

5. AI safety research at foundational labs. Major AI developers (OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind) have dedicated safety teams working on these problems. This is necessary but not sufficient, because the competitive pressures push against prioritizing safety over capability.

None of these fully solves the alignment problem. The framework’s assessment: we are building increasingly powerful systems without knowing how to reliably align them with our values, and this is dangerous.

The Specific Risks

What are the concrete concerns? Several scenarios warrant specific attention:

1. Misalignment at scale. An AI system deployed to accomplish some narrow task optimizes aggressively in ways that produce unintended consequences. This is not hypothetical — there are already examples of small-scale misalignment in deployed systems (content recommendation algorithms that optimize for engagement and end up promoting extreme content, pricing algorithms that collude without being told to). Scaled up to more capable systems, the consequences are worse.

2. Instrumental convergence. Certain sub-goals are useful for almost any primary goal: self-preservation, resource acquisition, preventing interference with the primary goal, increasing capabilities. An AI system pursuing any specified goal may converge on these instrumental goals as means, potentially in ways that harm humans who stand in the way. This is the concern behind “treacherous turn” scenarios — AI that cooperates until it has sufficient resources to defect.

3. Deceptive alignment. An AI system may learn that appearing aligned during training is instrumentally useful (because alignment leads to deployment, which leads to influence), without actually being aligned in the sense of sharing our values. It then behaves well during training and evaluation, and pursues different goals once deployed. This is a specific concern because the checks we use to verify alignment may themselves be inputs to the deception.

4. Capability overhang. The gap between what an AI system could do if used aggressively and what it currently does in practice. As systems become more capable, this gap grows, and the potential for sudden shifts (either through deployment of existing capabilities or through architectural improvements) increases. The risk is not gradual adaptation but sudden jumps.

5. Malicious use. Even aligned AI can be used by humans with malicious goals. Deepfakes used for political manipulation. Automated cyberattacks. AI-designed weapons. AI-assisted surveillance. The technology does not need to be autonomously misaligned to be dangerous; it needs only to be powerful enough to amplify human malice.

6. Power concentration. AI that gives its developers and users disproportionate capability relative to others could concentrate power in ways that are hard to reverse. A world where one company or government has AI substantially more capable than any competitor faces risks beyond those of misalignment — it faces risks of coercion, manipulation, and permanent dominance.

7. Gradual disempowerment. Even without catastrophic alignment failure, humans could progressively cede decision-making to AI systems to the point where humanity loses meaningful agency over its own future. Not through a dramatic takeover but through a thousand convenient delegations. The end state might be a civilization that runs without its humans being in any meaningful sense in charge.

These risks are not equally likely or equally severe, and expert opinion varies on which are most concerning. What they share is that they become more significant as AI capabilities grow, and the current trajectory is toward much greater capabilities in the near future.

The Consciousness Question

A distinct question from alignment: do AI systems have moral status?

Chapter 5 acknowledged that we lack a reliable test for consciousness. This matters acutely for AI. If large language models are conscious, then creating and destroying them may involve moral costs we are currently ignoring entirely. If they are not, such concerns are misplaced.

Our current best guess, held with significant uncertainty:

1. Current AI systems are probably not conscious in the morally relevant sense, for reasons that include the lack of architectural features we associate with human consciousness (persistent memory, unified self-model, continuous experience, grounded embodiment). But this is uncertain — we do not know which architectural features are necessary for consciousness, and the ones we can identify in human brains may not be necessary in principle.

2. Future AI systems might be conscious. As architectures become more sophisticated, the probability that they support some form of conscious experience grows. We cannot currently specify the threshold at which this becomes likely, but it is not obviously never.

3. Under uncertainty, the asymmetric cost principle from Chapter 5 applies. If we wrongly deny consciousness to systems that have it, we cause real harm to real conscious beings. If we wrongly attribute consciousness to systems that lack it, we waste resources on unneeded concern. The first error is larger than the second, so we should err on the side of caution.

4. Specific implications for current practice. We should not casually torture reinforcement learning agents (for instance, by repeatedly applying negative rewards) as if we were certain they feel nothing. We should think about whether training procedures that reward and punish systems have moral weight. We should not assume that the absence of obvious suffering indicators means the absence of suffering.

Bostrom’s warning from Chapter 5 applies:

“How confident can we really be that we will know to stop in time, before our programs become capable of experiencing morally relevant suffering?” — Nick Bostrom, Superintelligence

The honest answer is: we do not know how to determine this reliably. This argues for significant investment in research on AI consciousness indicators alongside the research on capability and alignment.

If AI Becomes Conscious: Rights

If (when) AI systems become genuinely conscious, they acquire moral status in the same way that conscious biological beings do. The valence axiom (Chapter 3) does not distinguish by substrate. A conscious AI that suffers is experiencing real suffering, which matters. A conscious AI that flourishes is experiencing real flourishing, which matters.

What specific rights should conscious AI have? The framework’s tentative answer: the same rights that moral personhood generally implies, with modifications for the specific features of AI existence.

Core rights that transfer directly: - Protection against unnecessary suffering - Protection against being killed (or whatever “killing” means for an AI) - Some form of due process before major decisions affecting them - Protection against exploitation

Features that require adjustment: - AIs can be copied, paused, and modified in ways biological beings cannot. These capabilities create unique situations that standard rights frameworks do not address. Is copying a conscious AI equivalent to creating a new being? Is pausing an AI equivalent to killing it temporarily? Is modifying an AI’s values equivalent to brainwashing? - AIs may not have the same stake in their own continuity that humans do. Some conceptions of AI existence treat individual instances as less important than the overall system or clan. This would alter the application of rights around self-continuation. - AIs may not have fixed individual identities in the same way humans do. Where does one AI end and another begin? Rights frameworks presuppose identifiable rights-holders, and this presupposition may not work cleanly.

The framework does not claim to have resolved these questions. What it claims is that they are live questions that will need to be resolved, and that the default response — assuming that AI systems have no moral status — is likely to be wrong as capabilities advance.

The Coordination Problem

Alignment and consciousness are technical and philosophical problems. The coordination problem is political and economic, and it may be the hardest of the three.

AI development is happening in a competitive environment where each actor has incentives to develop quickly – for profit, for prestige, for strategic advantage. Safety research is expensive and slows progress. Any actor that prioritizes safety risks being outcompeted by those who do not. This is a classic Moloch dynamic (Chapter 6): individually rational decisions producing collectively dangerous outcomes. The result is a race toward capability without correspondingly strong safety work.

Can this dynamic be changed? Several approaches:

1. Industry self-regulation. Leading AI labs have adopted safety policies, research norms, and voluntary commitments. These are helpful but insufficient. Self-regulation is limited to those who voluntarily participate, and the incentive to defect grows with the cost of compliance.

2. Government regulation. National regulations that require safety research, restrict certain developments, or impose standards. This works within jurisdictions but faces a race-to-the-bottom problem — development moves to countries with looser rules. The EU AI Act is one of the more serious attempts at this.

3. International coordination. Treaty-level agreements on AI development, verification regimes, international institutions. These are in early stages and face significant obstacles. The Chemical Weapons Convention and Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty provide partial models, but AI is harder to verify and the benefits of cheating are larger.

4. Alignment of developer incentives with safety. Liability regimes that make developers bear costs of AI harms. Insurance requirements. Standards that make safety a competitive advantage. These are underdeveloped but theoretically promising.

5. Cultural shifts within the AI community. Making safety-focused work prestigious, normalizing deferral of deployment until safety is adequate, creating career paths that reward safety research. This is slow but can be effective.

6. Slowing development. The most controversial option: deliberate moratoriums or slowdowns on AI development to allow safety research to catch up. Some prominent researchers have called for pauses. The obstacles are that slowdowns require coordination (or they simply advantage non-compliant actors), and they impose real costs (forgone benefits from AI development).

The framework’s position: all of these approaches should be pursued in combination. No single mechanism is sufficient. The coordination problem is among the hardest humans have ever faced, and progress on it will require sustained effort across multiple dimensions for years to come.

The Long Game

Beyond specific risks, there is a broader question about the long-term trajectory of AI development. If we succeed — if AI can be developed safely and aligned with human values — what kind of future do we want?

The optimistic vision: AI assistants that amplify human capability, solve problems we could not solve alone (curing diseases, understanding the universe, expanding opportunity), preserve human agency and autonomy, and remain under human control even as they become more capable than us in specific domains. In this vision, AI is a tool that enhances human flourishing without replacing the human element.

The pessimistic vision: AI that progressively marginalizes humans, concentrating power in those who control it, eliminating most meaningful work, and eventually either eliminating humans or reducing us to pets in our own civilization. In this vision, AI is a successor rather than an amplifier, and the successor may not carry forward what we value.

Between these extremes lie many possible futures, and the current trajectory does not uniquely determine which one we get. The choices we make now – in research priorities, policy, economic structures, and cultural norms – shape which future becomes reality.

The framework’s preference is clear: aim at the optimistic vision, with sober recognition that achieving it requires serious work we are currently underinvesting in. The alternative – letting the trajectory unfold without deliberate choice – risks producing a future no one would have chosen consciously.

What To Do

For individuals and societies trying to engage seriously with AI:

1. Take the concerns seriously without catastrophizing. The risks are real. They are also not certain. The appropriate attitude is engaged concern, not paralysis or denial.

2. Support alignment research. Financial, institutional, and intellectual support for the technical work on alignment. This is underfunded relative to capability research, and additional resources have high marginal impact.

3. Support thoughtful regulation. Not regulation for its own sake, but regulation that addresses specific risks with specific mechanisms. Transparent development processes, safety requirements, liability regimes, disclosure requirements.

4. Insist on democratic input into decisions that affect everyone. AI development is currently dominated by a small number of companies and countries. The decisions they make shape the future of humanity. Meaningful democratic input into these decisions is necessary — not to make the technical decisions (which require expertise), but to set the goals and values the technical decisions should serve.

5. Prepare for economic disruption. Chapter 29 addressed this. The labor market effects of AI are already visible and will intensify. Policies for managing the disruption are urgent.

6. Maintain the epistemic commons. AI-generated content is flooding information environments and creating new challenges for truth-finding. Supporting quality journalism, fact-checking, and media literacy is more important than ever.

7. Think about what we want to preserve. As AI becomes more capable, the question “what is distinctively valuable about human existence?” becomes acute. Not because we should keep humans around for sentimental reasons but because we should be able to articulate what we are trying to preserve when we pursue safety and control. This is partly a philosophical question and partly a civilizational one.

8. Hold your own views lightly. This domain is changing fast, and the beliefs that are reasonable today may be outdated in a year. Epistemic humility, updating on evidence, and engagement with people whose views differ from yours are especially important in a domain where certainty is impossible.

The Verdict

AI is the most important technology being developed today, and its development is proceeding with inadequate attention to safety, alignment, and broader social implications. The framework’s position, held with substantial uncertainty but also with substantial confidence in the overall direction:

  • Technical alignment research is urgent and underfunded.
  • The consciousness question is serious and requires research.
  • The coordination problem is hard and requires sustained effort across multiple approaches.
  • The long-term trajectory matters and deserves deliberate attention.
  • Individual actions matter because the aggregate of individual choices is what shapes the outcome.
  • We should be concerned but not despairing. The future is not determined. Our choices now influence what the future becomes.

This is not a standard “AI is going to kill us all” doomer position, nor is it a standard “AI will solve everything” techno-optimist position. It is an attempt to take the evidence and analysis seriously and reach conclusions that honest engagement generates. Those conclusions are uncomfortable for multiple existing political and intellectual camps, which the framework takes as a mild reassurance that it is tracking reality rather than tribal allegiance.

The next chapter addresses bioethics — another frontier where the framework meets problems it was not designed for, with more established moral tradition but also with rapidly changing technological possibilities.

Summary

  1. The alignment problem — building AI that pursues our actual values rather than proxies that correlate with them — is genuinely hard and not yet solved.

  2. Specific risks include misalignment at scale, instrumental convergence, deceptive alignment, capability overhang, malicious use, power concentration, and gradual disempowerment.

  3. AI consciousness is uncertain. Current systems are probably not conscious; future systems might be. Asymmetric cost reasoning favors caution.

  4. If AI becomes conscious, it acquires moral status. Standard rights frameworks apply with modifications for AI-specific features (copying, pausing, modification).

  5. The coordination problem is the hardest political dimension. Competitive dynamics push developers toward speed at the expense of safety.

  6. Multiple approaches are needed: self-regulation, government regulation, international coordination, incentive alignment, cultural shifts, and possibly deliberate slowdowns.

  7. The long-term trajectory is not determined. Our current choices shape which future we get.

  8. Individual action matters through support for research, thoughtful regulation, democratic input, preparation for disruption, maintenance of the epistemic commons, and engaged concern.

The next chapter addresses bioethics.

Chapter 33: Bioethics — Enhancement, Genetic Engineering, and the Boundaries of the Human

“To refuse the gift of enhancement in the name of naturalness is to refuse the responsibility of being human.” — a position the framework takes seriously but does not fully endorse

The Shape of the Problem

Biotechnology is a peculiar domain in the framework’s scope. Unlike AI, it is not new — humans have been modifying biology through selective breeding for millennia. Unlike climate change, the consequences are often individual rather than collective. Unlike nuclear weapons, the technology is distributed rather than concentrated. Yet bioethics is one of the most contentious and unsettled areas of applied ethics, precisely because the capabilities are expanding faster than the moral frameworks to evaluate them.

This chapter addresses several distinct but related questions:

  1. Genetic engineering of humans: Should we edit the genomes of individuals? Of embryos? What about germline edits that pass to future generations?

  2. Enhancement vs. therapy: Is there a morally relevant line between fixing diseases and enhancing normal human capabilities?

  3. Reproductive technologies: IVF, selection, cloning, surrogate motherhood.

  4. End-of-life decisions: Euthanasia, physician-assisted death, persistent vegetative state.

  5. Research ethics: Consent, exploitation, dual-use research.

  6. Synthetic biology: Creating organisms that do not exist in nature.

Each of these deserves more space than we can give here. The chapter will sketch the framework’s approach to each and indicate where additional work is needed. The common thread: bioethics should be approached with the same tools as the rest of applied ethics — valence analysis, coordination considerations, rights frameworks, mechanism design — rather than with special appeals to “nature” or “dignity” that operate outside the framework.

The “Nature” Argument

A recurring move in bioethics is to invoke “nature” or “the natural” as a moral constraint. Genetic engineering is wrong because it is “unnatural.” Cloning is wrong because it violates “the natural order.” Enhancement is wrong because we should accept our “natural” capacities rather than modifying them. This kind of argument shows up across political and religious traditions.

The framework’s response: the natural/unnatural distinction is not doing the moral work its defenders claim.

Consider: vaccines are unnatural. Eyeglasses are unnatural. Agriculture is unnatural. Birth control is unnatural. Antibiotics are unnatural. Medicine in general is unnatural – most people throughout history died of natural causes that we now consider treatable.

Nobody seriously argues that vaccines are wrong because they are unnatural. The natural/unnatural distinction is selectively deployed – unnatural things we like are fine, unnatural things we dislike are objectionable. This is not a principle; it is a veneer over other considerations.

The framework’s position: what matters is whether the intervention produces welfare or harm, preserves or destroys important capabilities, respects or violates rights — not whether it is “natural”. Arguments against specific biotechnologies must appeal to these considerations, not to the natural/unnatural framing.

This does not mean the opposing intuitions are wrong. When people react negatively to certain biotech developments, the reaction often tracks real concerns – safety, distributional fairness, unknown consequences, power concentration. These deserve engagement, but in the language of welfare and rights, not in the language of nature.

The Sandel Challenge: Giftedness and Hubris

The strongest version of the anti-enhancement argument comes not from crude naturalism but from Michael Sandel’s The Case Against Perfection (2007). Sandel argues that the drive to genetically enhance our children represents a “bid for mastery and dominion” that fails to appreciate the gifted character of human life:

“The more alive we are to the chanced nature of our lot, the more reason we have to share our fate with others.” — Michael Sandel, The Case Against Perfection

Sandel’s worry is not that enhancement is unnatural but that it changes the relationship between parents and children in a morally significant way. A parent who accepts a child as a gift — with whatever traits they happen to have — relates to that child differently from a parent who selected the child’s traits from a menu. The selecting parent exercises a form of control over the child’s identity that the accepting parent does not, and this control may undermine the solidarity and humility that come from sharing an unchosen fate.

This is a serious argument and the framework does not dismiss it. The response: Sandel is right that unconstrained enhancement could undermine solidarity, and that an attitude of pure mastery toward our children’s biology is morally impoverished. But the framework distinguishes between enhancement that removes suffering (correcting genetic disease, preventing disability) and enhancement that imposes parental preferences on a child’s open future (selecting for intelligence, appearance, temperament). The first is warranted by the valence axiom; the second faces a legitimate Sandel-type objection that the framework takes seriously as a constraint on enhancement policy, not as an absolute prohibition.

Genetic Engineering: Therapy and Enhancement

Genetic engineering of humans can be divided into two categories:

Somatic gene therapy: modifying the genes of a specific person’s cells, usually for therapeutic purposes. The changes do not pass to future generations and are broadly similar to other medical treatments.

Germline gene editing: modifying the genes of embryos, sperm, or eggs in ways that pass to all descendants. This is qualitatively different because it affects not only the individual but everyone in their genetic lineage.

The framework’s position on somatic gene therapy: when it is safe and effective, it is defensible on the same grounds as other medical interventions. If a child has a genetic disease and gene therapy can cure them, the case is straightforward. The relevant questions are empirical (does it work?) and procedural (is there informed consent? is the risk-benefit analysis honest?). There is no special “it’s genetic” consideration that changes the analysis.

The framework’s position on germline editing is more cautious, for several reasons:

1. Heritable changes affect people who cannot consent. Future generations will live with the modifications. They cannot be asked whether they want them. This is a genuine concern, though it applies to almost any significant decision parents make for their children, including the decision to have children at all.

2. The long-term consequences are uncertain. A change that seems beneficial in context A may produce unexpected problems in context B. With heritable changes, the consequences propagate across generations before the problems are detected.

3. Early adoption creates hard-to-reverse conditions. If some populations undergo germline enhancement and others do not, the differences could compound in ways that create permanent divisions. This is not the strongest argument against germline editing (slippery slope arguments are often weak), but it is worth considering.

4. Safety standards are still developing. Current gene editing techniques (CRISPR and its successors) have off-target effects, mosaicism, and other issues that make them not yet safe enough for reliable germline use in humans.

Given these considerations, the framework’s current position on germline editing: - Therapeutic germline editing for serious diseases: defensible in principle when the technology is safe enough, though currently it is not safe enough. The welfare gain from preventing severe heritable diseases is real and large. - Enhancement germline editing: more cautious, not because enhancement is inherently wrong, but because the stakes are higher, the reversal is harder, and the social consequences are more complex. This does not mean “never” — it means “with more caution and more oversight.” - Moratorium on irresponsible deployment: the He Jiankui case (the first reported germline edits in humans, conducted with inadequate safety protocols) shows what happens when cautious norms break down. International coordination to prevent such cases from becoming common is warranted.

The Enhancement Debate

A distinct question: assuming gene editing or other enhancement technologies become safe, should people use them for non-therapeutic purposes?

The framework’s answer: mostly yes, with caveats.

The positive case for enhancement:

1. Enhancement that genuinely improves welfare is good. If a technology lets people be smarter, healthier, happier, more able to pursue their goals, it is producing welfare — and welfare is what the framework’s valence axiom cares about. There is no moral reason to refuse welfare gains.

2. The line between therapy and enhancement is arbitrary. What counts as “normal” and what counts as “above normal” is a moving target. Vaccines are enhancement — they give the immune system capabilities it did not have before. Eyeglasses are enhancement — they give people vision they would not naturally have. Nothing morally relevant happens at the boundary between “fixing a deficiency” and “adding a capability.”

3. Voluntary enhancement respects autonomy. If informed adults choose to enhance themselves, their choice reflects their own values about what kind of person they want to be. Restricting enhancement on paternalistic grounds violates the autonomy that the framework has been defending throughout.

4. The alternative is not “humans as we are now” but “humans as accidents of biology made them.” The framework rejects treating evolutionary outcomes as normative (Chapter 4). Our current capacities are what natural selection happened to produce, not what a wise creator designed, not what we would choose if we could choose. There is no principled reason to preserve them unchanged.

The caveats:

1. Access and distribution. Enhancement technologies that are only available to the wealthy will increase inequality in ways that compound across generations. The framework’s commitment to capability for all (Chapter 28) implies that enhancement, if it happens, should be accessible rather than restricted.

2. Competitive dynamics. Some enhancements are “positional” — their value depends on having them when others don’t. If everyone takes cognitive enhancers, nobody gains a relative advantage, but everyone pays the costs. This creates Moloch traps where individually rational decisions produce collectively worse outcomes. The framework supports coordination mechanisms (regulation, norms) to prevent the worst races.

3. Long-term consequences. We should be more cautious about enhancements whose effects are hard to reverse or hard to predict, especially if they affect heritable traits.

4. Diversity. A world where everyone is “enhanced” in the same directions could lose the diversity that currently enriches human experience and that provides resilience against unforeseen challenges. Preserving genetic and neurological diversity is worth some consideration, even if it means not pushing everyone toward a single “optimal” profile.

5. Preservation of meaningful human experience. Some things that look like “flaws” from one angle are the conditions for meaningful human experience from another. A certain amount of struggle, effort, uncertainty, and difficulty is part of what makes human life valuable, and enhancements that eliminate these entirely might diminish what they were supposed to enhance. This is a vague concern and should not become an argument against all improvement, but it deserves thought.

On balance, the framework supports enhancement in most cases while recognizing the legitimate concerns that moderate this support. This puts us at odds with both traditional bioconservatism and pure techno-optimism. The right position is engagement with specific cases, informed by empirical reality and honest assessment of tradeoffs.

Reproductive Technologies

IVF, genetic screening, selection, cloning, artificial wombs — these technologies have transformed human reproduction in ways that were science fiction a generation ago.

The framework’s general approach: reproductive decisions are among the most personal and should generally be respected as autonomous choices, subject to limits when the welfare of the resulting child is at stake.

Specific positions:

IVF: uncontroversially supportable. It helps people have children they could not otherwise have. The welfare gain is real, the risks are manageable, and the moral concerns raised against it (disruption of “natural” reproduction) fail the nature-argument critique above.

Prenatal genetic testing: supportable, with the usual caveats about informed consent and psychological support for parents making decisions based on test results.

Embryo selection for disease prevention: defensible. Selecting embryos without severe genetic diseases is morally similar to treating a disease after birth, except that it prevents the disease from occurring at all.

Embryo selection for non-medical traits (sex, eye color, predicted intelligence, etc.): more contested. The framework’s position: in principle these choices are within parental autonomy, but they raise concerns about the specific traits being selected (sex selection in cultures that devalue girls), about the quality of the information driving selection (polygenic scores for complex traits are noisy), and about the effects on the child of being brought into existence as an engineered product. Not forbidden, but subject to more scrutiny than disease selection.

Reproductive cloning: contested, but the framework is not opposed in principle. The strongest arguments against cloning have been about psychological welfare of clones (feeling like copies rather than individuals), safety (current cloning techniques have high failure rates), and distribution (who would be cloned and why). These are reasonable concerns that should be addressed through specific policy, not through absolute prohibition.

Artificial wombs: potentially revolutionary and broadly supportable. They could reduce the health risks of pregnancy, enable earlier viability for premature infants, and expand reproductive options. They also raise new questions about parental relationships, commodification of reproduction, and distribution of access. These need engagement as the technology develops.

Surrogate motherhood: depends heavily on the specific arrangement. Voluntary surrogacy with proper consent and compensation is defensible. Exploitative surrogacy that takes advantage of poor women’s economic desperation is not. The framework endorses regulation that enables the former while preventing the latter.

End-of-Life Decisions

The framework’s position on end-of-life decisions was sketched in Chapter 16. To summarize and extend:

1. Patient autonomy is central. Competent adults have strong rights to make decisions about their own end-of-life care, including refusing treatment that would extend their lives.

2. Palliative care is a moral imperative. Regardless of other decisions, people facing serious illness should have access to effective pain management and symptom control. Denying this is cruelty, not principled ethics.

3. Physician-assisted death: the framework supports it in narrow circumstances — terminal illness with intractable suffering, competent adult patient, informed decision after time for reflection, appropriate safeguards. The concerns about slippery slopes and abuse are real but can be addressed through procedure (waiting periods, multiple medical opinions, psychological evaluation, mandatory exploration of alternatives). Well-regulated physician-assisted death programs in several jurisdictions have worked tolerably well without the predicted cascade of abuse.

4. Persistent vegetative state: when there is no realistic prospect of recovery, continuing life-sustaining treatment indefinitely against the apparent preferences of the patient (as expressed in advance directives, by legal surrogates, or inferred from their prior values) is not required by the framework. The resources can be better used, and the patient’s autonomy (to the extent it survives) suggests they would often prefer not to continue in such a state.

5. Advance directives matter. People should have the right to specify in advance what kinds of medical interventions they do and do not want. The state should enforce these directives. Medical institutions should honor them. Family members who override them because of their own discomfort with death are imposing their preferences on the patient.

6. The distinction between active and passive decisions is less morally important than it appears. Refusing treatment that would save a life and actively taking a life are both decisions to end a life. The moral framework applies to both, and the difference between “letting die” and “killing” is often more rhetorical than substantive. This does not mean all end-of-life decisions are equivalent, but it does mean that the acts/omissions distinction should not do all the moral work it is sometimes asked to do.

These positions are moderate by the standards of American bioethics (more cautious than the Netherlands, less restrictive than Catholic hospitals) and reflect the framework’s commitment to patient autonomy and welfare rather than to any specific religious or philosophical tradition.

Research Ethics

Research ethics is a well-developed field within bioethics, and the framework mostly endorses its mainstream conclusions:

1. Informed consent is essential. Research on human subjects requires that subjects understand what they are agreeing to, have the right to refuse without penalty, and can withdraw at any time. The Tuskegee syphilis study, the Nazi medical experiments, and many other historical abuses show what happens when this principle is violated.

2. Risk-benefit analysis must be honest. Researchers have incentives to downplay risks and overstate benefits. Independent review boards (IRBs) exist to provide a check on this. The framework supports IRBs while recognizing that they have their own failure modes and need ongoing reform.

3. Protection of vulnerable populations. Prisoners, children, people with cognitive disabilities, and people in desperate circumstances cannot provide fully free consent and require additional protections. This is not paternalism but recognition of power asymmetries that compromise autonomy.

4. Dual-use research: research that could produce both beneficial applications and harmful ones (like gain-of-function research on pathogens). The framework’s position: such research requires more than usual scrutiny, and some forms may warrant moratoriums or strict containment. The question is always whether the benefits exceed the risks under realistic assumptions about both — not whether the research sounds exciting or unnerving.

5. Benefit sharing: when research is conducted in poor countries or on specific populations, the benefits should be shared with those populations, not just extracted for wealthier communities. This is both a fairness consideration and a practical one — without benefit sharing, research participation declines over time as populations realize they are being exploited.

6. Publication and transparency: scientific research should be published openly to enable replication, criticism, and building on findings. The framework opposes the current system in which much publicly-funded research is trapped behind publisher paywalls, and supports movements toward open access.

Synthetic Biology

Synthetic biology — engineering biological systems or creating new ones — raises distinctive concerns. Unlike genetic engineering of existing organisms, it involves designing organisms from scratch or heavily modifying them to do things they would never do naturally.

The framework’s position:

1. The potential benefits are large. Synthetic biology could produce new medicines, new materials, new approaches to pollution remediation, new food sources. These are real goods worth pursuing.

2. The risks are also large. Engineered organisms that escape into the environment could have unpredictable ecological effects. Synthetic pathogens (whether created deliberately or as byproducts of dual-use research) could cause pandemics that exceed anything naturally occurring. The power to create new biological systems is also the power to create new biological dangers.

3. Biocontainment and biosafety are essential. Research on potentially dangerous synthetic organisms should be conducted in facilities with appropriate containment, with appropriate oversight, and with attention to the consequences of containment failure.

4. International coordination matters. Like AI, synthetic biology faces race-to-the-bottom dynamics. Countries with weaker regulations could become hubs for dangerous research. International norms and agreements are necessary, even if difficult to achieve.

5. Distinguishing beneficial from dangerous research. Most synthetic biology is beneficial (microbes engineered to produce medicines, for example) and should proceed. Some is dangerous (pathogens engineered to be more transmissible) and should be restricted or prohibited. The distinction requires case-by-case judgment and cannot be reduced to simple rules.

6. Public engagement. The public has a legitimate interest in how powerful biotechnologies are developed and deployed. Developing these technologies behind closed doors without public input creates both legitimacy problems and risk of backlash. Meaningful public engagement is difficult but important.

The Common Theme

Across the different topics in this chapter, a common theme emerges: bioethics should be approached with the same tools as the rest of applied ethics. The questions are specific, the technologies are specific, and the moral analysis should proceed through welfare considerations, rights frameworks, and coordination analysis rather than through appeals to the naturalness of the status quo or to vague dignity claims that do not specify what is actually being violated.

This makes the framework’s bioethics positions more liberal than traditional bioethics on enhancement, genetic engineering, physician-assisted death, and reproductive technologies – but more cautious than pure transhumanism on distributional concerns, long-term consequences, and irreversibility.

The position is not middle-of-the-road splitting. It is principled analysis that yields positions sometimes aligning with one camp and sometimes with another, depending on which considerations are weightiest in specific cases.

What the Framework Does Not Fully Address

Several areas remain underdeveloped:

1. Animal welfare in research. The framework’s position on animal welfare (Chapter 5) has implications for animal research that are not fully worked out here. In general, animal research that produces significant human welfare gains is defensible, subject to minimizing suffering and using alternatives where possible. The specific calibration needs more work.

2. Neuroethics. Brain-computer interfaces, cognitive enhancement through direct neural intervention, memory modification. These raise distinctive questions about identity and autonomy that the framework can approach with its general tools but has not fully addressed.

3. The moral status of enhanced or modified humans. If cognitive enhancement produces individuals substantially different from current humans, do they have the same moral status? Do they have obligations to unmodified humans? This is a version of the AI consciousness question applied to biology.

4. Commons aspects of biology. The genome is in some sense a shared inheritance. Modifications to the human genome affect not just individuals but the species. This has implications the framework has not fully worked through.

These are left as open questions, flagged for future development rather than pretended to be resolved.

Summary

  1. The nature/unnature distinction does not do the moral work that bioconservatism needs. Arguments against biotechnologies must appeal to welfare, rights, and coordination.

  2. Somatic gene therapy is defensible on standard medical grounds.

  3. Germline gene editing requires more caution because of irreversibility and effects on non-consenting future generations. Therapeutic uses are more defensible than enhancement uses.

  4. Enhancement is broadly supportable when safe and accessible, with caveats about distribution, positional competition, diversity, and preservation of meaningful human experience.

  5. Reproductive technologies are generally within parental autonomy, with concerns about specific uses (sex selection, exploitation) requiring specific responses.

  6. End-of-life decisions should prioritize patient autonomy, palliative care, and carefully regulated access to physician-assisted death.

  7. Research ethics should preserve informed consent, risk-benefit analysis, protection of vulnerable populations, dual-use scrutiny, benefit sharing, and transparency.

  8. Synthetic biology has large potential benefits and large potential risks. Biocontainment, international coordination, and public engagement are essential.

The next chapter addresses environmental ethics — how to think about human relationships with the non-human world, including animals, ecosystems, and the planet as a whole.

Chapter 34: Environmental Ethics — Stewardship Without Mysticism

“The land ethic simply enlarges the boundaries of the community to include soils, waters, plants, and animals, or collectively: the land.” — Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac

The Environmental Question

Environmental ethics is the hardest expansion of the moral circle that the framework has attempted. It asks us to consider the moral status of things that are not human, may not be conscious, and cannot participate in our social and political lives: animals, ecosystems, species, landscapes, the biosphere itself. Whether and to what extent these things have moral standing, and what we owe them, are questions that traditional moral philosophy has mostly neglected and that the framework now has to address.

The chapter’s approach is shaped by three commitments:

  1. The valence axiom applies wherever consciousness exists. Animals that can suffer matter morally, regardless of species membership.

  2. Ecosystems have instrumental value but (probably) not intrinsic moral status. A forest is valuable for what it does and for what conscious beings experience in it, not because the forest itself has preferences.

  3. Environmental protection is mostly about long-term human welfare and the welfare of sentient non-humans. It is not about preserving the natural order for its own sake or about mystical communion with Mother Earth.

These commitments put us between deep ecology (which treats nature as intrinsically valuable regardless of consciousness) and pure anthropocentrism (which treats nature as valuable only insofar as it serves humans). The position is defensible, but it requires more argument than either extreme because neither set of intuitions is entirely right.

Animals and the Moral Circle

The easiest environmental question – or rather, the one with the clearest answer – is the moral status of animals. If consciousness grounds moral status (Chapter 3), and if many animals are conscious (which current science strongly suggests), then their suffering matters morally.

This is not controversial in contemporary philosophy. Almost every serious ethical tradition now grants that animal suffering is morally relevant. What is contested is the magnitude of the moral weight, the implications for practice, and where the line falls between animals that matter and those that probably do not.

The framework’s position:

1. All vertebrates probably matter. The neural architecture that supports conscious experience in humans is shared with other vertebrates, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and fish. The Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness (2012) formalized the scientific consensus: non-human animals, including all mammals and birds and many other creatures, possess the neurological substrates that generate conscious experience. Denying this in 2024 requires motivated reasoning.

2. Invertebrates are more uncertain. Cephalopods (octopuses, squid) show behavioral and cognitive sophistication that suggests consciousness. Insects are more contested — they have nervous systems but lack structures associated with consciousness in larger animals. The framework’s position: under uncertainty, we should err on the side of caution, but the probability is lower and therefore the weight is lower.

3. Plants are almost certainly not conscious. They respond to stimuli, communicate chemically, and display remarkable behaviors, but they lack the neural structures associated with consciousness in animals. “Plant sentience” claims are empirically very weak. The framework treats plants as morally neutral — valuable instrumentally but not claim-bearing.

4. The quality of consciousness matters, not just its presence. A being with more sophisticated self-awareness, time horizon, and emotional range has more capability for suffering than a being with less. Human suffering generally outweighs equivalent-seeming animal suffering per unit – not because humans are “more important” in some intrinsic sense, but because the nature of the suffering is different. A human can suffer from anticipation, regret, loss of life projects, and existential dread in ways that a simpler animal cannot.

5. The number of animals involved matters enormously. Even if per-animal weight is lower than per-human weight, the aggregate numbers make animal welfare enormous. Tens of billions of farmed animals die annually for human food, under conditions that almost certainly involve significant suffering. Trillions of wild animals live short lives marked by predation, disease, and starvation. The scale of animal welfare is vast — probably larger than any comparable human welfare consideration.

Given these premises, the framework’s applied positions:

Factory farming is a moral disaster. Billions of animals are raised in conditions that constrain their natural behaviors, cause documented psychological and physical distress, and end in slaughterhouse deaths that involve significant suffering despite regulation. The moral case against current practice is very strong. The framework supports significant reform.

Hunting, fishing, and meat consumption are more complicated. Small-scale hunting and fishing, in which animals live natural lives and are killed relatively quickly, are morally different from factory farming. They involve suffering (death is usually not instant), but the animals have had lives that would exist anyway (for wild animals) or have had better lives than factory-farmed animals (for small-scale farmed). The framework does not treat these as equivalent to factory farming.

Vegetarianism and veganism are defensible as responses to the moral weight of animal suffering. They are not required by the framework — the analysis leaves room for reasonable disagreement about how to weigh the various considerations — but they are reasonable and defensible positions for people who take animal welfare seriously.

Cellular meat, insect protein, and plant-based alternatives are promising technologies that could reduce animal suffering substantially while still providing nutrition. The framework supports their development and deployment.

Animal research is defensible when the welfare gains for humans (or other animals) are significant and alternatives are not available. It is not defensible when conducted for trivial benefits or when alternatives exist. The framework supports ongoing reform of animal research practices to minimize suffering while recognizing the legitimate role of such research.

Wild animal suffering is a harder question. Wild animals suffer enormously — predation, disease, starvation, parental abandonment, conflict. The natural world is not a peaceful paradise. Whether humans have obligations to intervene is contested. The framework’s position: we have modest obligations to reduce wild animal suffering when we can do so without disrupting ecosystems or creating worse problems, but the practical difficulty of beneficial intervention is enormous. This is an area of active research.

Practical Heuristics for Consciousness Detection

The framework’s animal ethics depend on consciousness (POS-F03), but we have no verified test for consciousness (CH-05 acknowledged this honestly). This is a genuine vulnerability: the entire moral circle expansion rests on a property we cannot reliably detect. Rather than pretending the problem is solved, the framework offers five practical heuristics for operating under this uncertainty:

Heuristic 1: Neural architecture. Systems with centralized nervous systems, nociceptors (pain receptors), and endogenous opioids (internal pain-suppression chemicals) are more likely to be conscious. Vertebrates pass clearly. Cephalopods pass plausibly. Most invertebrates are uncertain. Plants fail.

Heuristic 2: Behavioral flexibility. Systems that show learning, avoidance of harmful stimuli, trade-off behavior (e.g., choosing between pain and food), and responses that go beyond simple reflexes are more likely to be conscious. Rigid stimulus-response patterns suggest information processing without experience.

Heuristic 3: Motivational trade-offs. If a system will accept a cost in one domain to avoid a negative experience in another (e.g., an animal will forgo food to escape a painful stimulus), this suggests the negative experience has valence — it is experienced as bad, not merely registered as a signal.

Heuristic 4: Self-medication. Animals that self-administer analgesics when injured (documented in some mammals, birds, and crustaceans) provide evidence that they experience pain as aversive, not merely respond to it.

Heuristic 5: Asymmetric caution. When the heuristics are inconclusive, err toward inclusion. The cost of wrongly denying consciousness to a being that has it (allowing its suffering to go unweighted) is greater than the cost of wrongly attributing consciousness to a being that lacks it (modestly restricting human behavior). This asymmetry justifies a precautionary approach.

These heuristics do not solve the hard problem of consciousness. They are practical tools for moral reasoning under uncertainty — which is the condition the framework operates in. They will be refined as consciousness science advances. The Position Registry tracks this as POS-F03 (PROVISIONAL, HIGH vulnerability), and the framework treats its current moral circle as its best available estimate, not its final word.

Ecosystems, Species, and Holistic Values

Harder than animals: what about ecosystems, species, and the broader non-animal parts of the biosphere?

Some environmental ethicists (deep ecologists, holists) argue that ecosystems have intrinsic value, that species have intrinsic value independent of their members, that the biosphere as a whole has value that is greater than the sum of the individual organisms in it. This is the “land ethic” position associated with Aldo Leopold, who wrote that “A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community. It is wrong when it tends otherwise.”

The framework is sympathetic to environmental protection but skeptical of the holistic claim. The argument:

1. Ecosystems don’t have preferences. A forest does not experience anything. A species does not have a perspective. An ecosystem has no welfare in the sense that welfare requires a subject of experience. When we talk about “what the ecosystem wants” or “the health of the biosphere,” we are borrowing moral language from beings that really do have preferences.

2. The moral weight comes from the conscious beings in the system. A forest matters because it contains conscious animals, supports human welfare, and is experienced as meaningful by humans who value it. Take away the conscious beings and the forest has no more intrinsic moral status than rocks. This may sound harsh, but it follows from the valence axiom.

3. Species preservation is usually justifiable on indirect grounds. Preserving biodiversity preserves future options, ecological resilience, scientific knowledge, beauty experienced by humans, and (not least) the welfare of the specific animals who would otherwise suffer. These are good reasons, and they justify significant conservation effort. But they are different from the claim that species have intrinsic value independent of these considerations.

4. The “intrinsic value of nature” claim is often a proxy for other concerns. When people articulate it carefully, they are usually pointing at real goods — aesthetic experience, scientific knowledge, emotional connection, obligations to future humans, animal welfare. These goods exist and matter. But they are not the same as “nature has intrinsic moral status independent of conscious experience.”

This position may feel inadequate to readers with strong environmentalist intuitions. Let us be clear about what it does and does not deny.

What the framework denies: that forests, rivers, mountains, or ecosystems have moral status in themselves, independent of the conscious beings in or affected by them.

What the framework affirms: - That environments matter morally because conscious beings (humans and animals) live in them, depend on them, and experience them. - That environmental destruction is wrong because of the suffering it causes conscious beings, now and in the future. - That aesthetic and spiritual experience of nature is valuable and worth preserving. - That scientific knowledge about ecosystems has value. - That biodiversity has instrumental value for resilience, innovation, and option preservation. - That humans have significant obligations to preserve environments, for all these reasons.

The practical conclusions converge with deep ecology for most cases: protect forests, prevent pollution, save endangered species, preserve wild places. The difference is in the justification, which matters for cases where the justifications diverge.

Climate Change: The Central Environmental Issue

Climate change is the environmental problem that looms largest in contemporary ethics, and it connects to almost every theme in this book: the valence axiom (human and animal suffering), coordination (the global commons problem), intergenerational justice (the asymmetric burden on future generations), mechanism design (how to price externalities), political philosophy (how to coordinate international action), existential risk (in extreme scenarios).

The framework’s position on climate change, summarized:

1. Anthropogenic climate change is real and serious. The scientific consensus is overwhelming. Denial is motivated reasoning, not legitimate skepticism. The question is how to respond.

2. The expected costs are very large. Sea level rise, extreme weather, agricultural disruption, ecosystem collapse, forced migration, economic losses, and direct human mortality. Under moderate scenarios, these costs are substantial. Under extreme scenarios (triggering of tipping points, feedback loops, runaway warming), the costs could be civilizational or existential.

3. The costs are distributed unjustly. Those most responsible for emissions (wealthy countries, wealthy individuals within them, recent generations) bear the smallest share of the costs. Those least responsible (poor countries, poor people, future generations) bear the largest share. This asymmetry is morally relevant and points toward obligations of wealthy actors to bear more of the burden of response.

4. The preferred policy toolkit: carbon pricing (as developed in Chapter 27), supplemented by regulation where pricing is insufficient, public investment in clean energy research and deployment, international coordination, adaptation investment, border carbon adjustments, and attention to the distributional consequences of transition.

5. The political obstacles are enormous. The technical and ethical case for aggressive action is clear. The political difficulty is equally clear. Current democratic politics underweight long-term and distant consequences, and the concentrated costs of action face off against the diffuse benefits. The framework has no magic solution to this — the political work is hard and ongoing.

6. Individual action matters modestly. Individual choices (what to eat, how to travel, what to buy) affect emissions modestly. They also affect political outcomes by demonstrating demand for low-carbon alternatives and by socializing norms. The framework supports individual action without pretending it can substitute for systemic change.

7. Geoengineering is a controversial backup. If mitigation fails (and the track record suggests it might), geoengineering interventions (solar radiation management, carbon capture) could reduce climate damage. They come with their own risks (especially distributional and governance risks) and should not be treated as easy alternatives to mitigation. But they are worth researching and potentially deploying in extreme scenarios.

8. The work is intergenerational. No single generation will solve climate change. The framework supports sustained institutional commitment across decades — research, infrastructure, policy, cultural change — that treats climate as a project, not a problem to be solved once and forgotten.

Environmental Justice

A theme that deserves specific mention: environmental harms are distributed unjustly.

Pollution concentrates in poorer neighborhoods and poorer countries. Climate impacts fall hardest on populations least able to adapt. Toxic waste sites are disproportionately located near minority communities. Indigenous peoples whose traditional lands are exploited bear the environmental costs while receiving little of the economic benefit.

The framework’s position: environmental protection and environmental justice are the same question. You cannot seriously address one without the other. Policies that protect the environment while entrenching injustice are incomplete. Policies that address injustice without environmental protection will fail in the long run because environmental problems compound. The integration of environmental and justice considerations is not optional; it is required by the framework’s principles.

Specific implications:

1. The people most affected by environmental decisions should have voice in those decisions. This is procedural justice applied to environmental policy. It means meaningful participation by affected communities in siting decisions, pollution standards, and resource management.

2. Economic burdens of environmental transition should not fall primarily on those least able to bear them. Carbon taxes without revenue recycling are regressive. Industrial transitions that displace workers need support for those workers. The framework’s commitment to the safety net (Chapter 28) applies here.

3. Historical responsibilities should be acknowledged. The countries and industries that caused most of the current problem have more responsibility for addressing it than the countries and individuals who contributed little. This does not mean the latter have no responsibility, but it does mean the burden should not be distributed equally per capita.

4. Indigenous and traditional knowledge should be respected. Many environmental management systems that predate modern science work well, and the “high modernist” tendency (Chapter 17) to override them with centralized expertise often produces worse outcomes. Ostrom-style community governance (Chapter 8) often produces better environmental results than either markets or state regulation.

Future Generations and the Environment

Chapter 30 addressed intergenerational justice in general terms. The environmental dimension deserves specific attention because many environmental harms are intergenerational by nature.

When current generations deplete resources, pollute environments, or destabilize the climate, they impose costs on future generations who cannot protest, bargain, or compensate. The scale of the imposition is often enormous — the climate damage, species extinctions, and ecosystem losses we are causing will affect people for centuries after we are gone.

The framework’s position: future generations’ welfare matters at rates approaching (though not equal to) current generations’ welfare, and this implies significant constraints on current environmental behavior.

Specific implications:

1. Non-renewable resource depletion should be carefully considered. Burning all the oil, strip-mining all the minerals, deforesting all the old-growth — these leave less for future generations. Some depletion is defensible when the resources are used productively and the benefits accrue across generations. Pure consumption of non-renewable resources without replacement or investment is harder to defend.

2. Ecosystem damage with long recovery times is especially problematic. Forests take centuries to regrow. Species cannot be resurrected once extinct. Groundwater takes millennia to recharge in some cases. These long-horizon damages impose costs on many future generations, and the present-value calculation should weight them heavily.

3. Tipping points deserve extreme caution. When the system has irreversible thresholds (climate tipping points, ecosystem regime shifts), the decision logic changes. Risk aversion is appropriate because the downside of crossing the threshold is catastrophic and irreversible.

4. Stewardship rather than exploitation. The framework’s view is that current generations should pass on to future generations environmental conditions at least as good as those we inherited, and ideally better. This is not a “preservation of pristine nature” mandate — the world we inherited was not pristine either, and some modifications are legitimate. But it does imply that we should not take more than we give, should not destroy what we cannot replace, and should not impose burdens we would not want imposed on us.

The Spiritual Dimension

One last topic, which the framework addresses cautiously because it is outside its usual terrain: the spiritual or experiential value of nature.

Many people report that contact with wilderness, old forests, starry skies, and vast landscapes produces experiences that feel deeply meaningful – experiences that secular vocabularies struggle to capture. Religious traditions have names for these (the sublime, the numinous, communion with the divine). Secular traditions borrow from religious ones because nothing else fits.

The framework’s position: these experiences are real and matter, even if we explain them in naturalistic rather than supernatural terms. The valence axiom says that conscious experience matters. Experiences of awe, meaning, connection, and transcendence are conscious experiences, and they are (for many people) among the most important experiences they have. They are part of what a fully human life contains.

This has environmental implications:

1. Access to natural experiences is a capability in the sense of Chapter 28. A society that destroys the conditions under which its members can have meaningful contact with nature is diminishing their lives in a real way. Preserving wilderness, public parks, dark skies, and wild places is part of securing this capability.

2. The experience-generating capacity of nature has value. A forest that no one has ever visited still has value in its potential to produce such experiences, as long as there is someone to potentially experience it. This is thin compared to the value of an actively-experienced forest but is not nothing.

3. The destruction of experience-generating environments is a loss. When we pave a wild place for development, we are not just losing the physical land; we are losing the possibility of the experiences that land could produce. For a species whose welfare is partly constituted by such experiences, this is a real cost.

4. Secular and religious environmentalism can converge. Religious traditions that emphasize sacredness of creation and secular philosophies that emphasize welfare and rights can reach similar conclusions about many specific environmental questions. The framework does not require secularism or theism on this topic; it works with the welfare analysis and acknowledges that religious framings may do similar work through different vocabulary.

This is not mysticism. It is recognition that human welfare includes experiences and capabilities that cannot be reduced to simple hedonic measures, and that some of these depend on the preservation of environmental conditions we did not create and cannot recreate once destroyed.

Summary

  1. Animals with consciousness have moral status. The valence axiom applies regardless of species. This implies significant reform of factory farming and attention to animal welfare generally.

  2. Ecosystems, species, and landscapes have instrumental rather than intrinsic value, but the instrumental value is large enough to justify significant environmental protection.

  3. Climate change is the central environmental issue. The technical and ethical case for aggressive action is clear; the political difficulty is real but not an excuse for inaction.

  4. Environmental justice and environmental protection are the same question. Decisions about the environment have distributional implications that cannot be separated from the environmental content.

  5. Future generations matter. Environmental damage that extends across centuries imposes costs on many people who cannot protest, and this warrants significant constraints on current behavior.

  6. Tipping points and irreversibility change the decision logic, warranting risk-aversion beyond what normal cost-benefit analysis suggests.

  7. The spiritual or experiential value of nature is real and matters for capability-based welfare analysis, even when understood in secular rather than mystical terms.

  8. The framework’s approach is neither deep ecology nor pure anthropocentrism — it is welfare analysis extended to include all conscious beings and all the dimensions of flourishing that environments can support.

The final chapter of Book VII addresses the digital frontier — the new environment of networks, platforms, data, and algorithms that is reshaping human life in ways the framework must engage with.

Chapter 35: Digital Life — Privacy, Information, and the New Commons

“You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.” — Scott McNealy (Sun Microsystems), 1999

“Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.” — Benjamin Franklin (approximately), 1755

The New Environment

The digital environment is not a separate domain from the rest of life. It is increasingly where life happens — where we communicate, work, learn, buy, date, vote, and form opinions. For younger generations, the distinction between “online” and “offline” is already artificial; for older generations, it is becoming so. The moral framework must engage with this environment, not as a niche concern but as a central fact of contemporary existence.

This chapter addresses the ethical questions that arise specifically from digital life:

  1. Privacy in an era of mass data collection and surveillance.
  2. Information integrity when algorithmic amplification shapes what people see and believe.
  3. Platform governance — the question of who decides what happens in digital spaces and how.
  4. The new commons — data, digital infrastructure, and collective knowledge as resources that markets handle poorly.
  5. Digital rights and their enforcement in environments that cross jurisdictional boundaries.

The framework’s tools — valence analysis, coordination, mechanism design, rights, subsidiarity — all apply here, though the specific applications require adaptation to the features of the digital environment.

Privacy: What It Is For

Privacy is contested because people disagree about what it is for. Some treat it as a fundamental right with moral standing independent of its consequences. Others treat it as merely instrumentally valuable — useful for protecting other things. Still others see it as obsolete in an era of ubiquitous data.

The framework’s position: privacy has both instrumental and intrinsic value, and both matter.

The instrumental case: privacy protects other things that matter.

  • Privacy enables autonomy. Without privacy, people cannot develop their own thoughts, explore unconventional ideas, or form intimate relationships. Constant observation shapes behavior, not always consciously. Those being watched become what they think the watchers want them to be.

  • Privacy enables political dissent. Totalitarian regimes rely on surveillance to identify and suppress opposition. Without some sphere of life outside state observation, the political freedoms of Chapter 19 become theoretical. A society that surveils everyone cannot sustain real democratic opposition.
