Rawls’s framework is largely static — what a just society looks like at a point in time. It handles change and dynamism less well. - Address non-citizens. The original position assumes the participants are all in the same society. Questions about people outside the society (immigrants, foreigners, future generations) are handled awkwardly.

The framework uses the original position as one tool among several, not as the foundational device it is for Rawls.

The Framework’s Political Philosophy, Restated

The framework’s political philosophy (developed in Book V) can be compared to Rawls directly:

On basic liberties: agreement with Rawls that these take priority and cannot be traded off against aggregate welfare, though we ground them in coordination considerations rather than in pure agreement behind a veil.

On fair equality of opportunity: agreement with Rawls that positions should be genuinely open to all, combined with attention to the capability considerations Sen raised.

On distribution: we reject the strong difference principle but accept that the worst off deserve special consideration. Our position is between Rawls and pure utilitarianism.

On the basic structure: agreement that institutions matter morally, combined with specific attention to how institutions actually function (mechanism design, not just pattern-specification).

On public reason: agreement that political argument should use reasons that can be shared across ideological lines, combined with honest acknowledgment of broader commitments when relevant.

On production as well as distribution: the framework cares about work, meaning, and the structure of economic life in ways Rawls does not fully address.

On moral epistemology: agreement on reflective equilibrium as the method, combined with more attention to empirical considerations (game theory, psychology, history).

The overall position is recognizable as Rawlsian in its broad structure but differs in specific details. The framework is what you might get if you started with Rawls and adjusted to accommodate the capability critique, the coordination analysis, the concerns about production, and the empirical grounding of Book I.

The Verdict

Rawls is the rival the framework respects most. His insights are real, his arguments are serious, and his influence on the framework is significant. Where we disagree, the disagreement is specific and substantive, not fundamental. A person who accepts Rawls’s framework and then carefully engages with the considerations in Book I and elsewhere would likely arrive at something close to the framework’s position.

This chapter has not refuted Rawls — his position remains defensible in its main outlines. What it has done is identify the specific adjustments the framework makes and explain why. The result is a political philosophy that is Rawlsian in structure but modified by considerations Rawls did not fully engage with.

If you want to call the framework a form of “modified Rawlsianism,” that is not quite right (because we differ on several specific points), but it is closer to the truth than calling it Kantian or utilitarian would be. The debt to Rawls is the largest of any contemporary philosopher, and the engagement with him is the most sustained.

Summary

  1. Rawls’s contract argument derives principles of justice from the choices rational agents would make behind a veil of ignorance. This is the most powerful framework in contemporary political philosophy.

  2. The framework agrees with Rawls on the importance of basic structure, the utility of original-position reasoning, the priority of basic liberties, the special status of the worst off, impartiality in institutional design, and reflective equilibrium as method.

  3. The framework disagrees with Rawls on maximin reasoning (we prefer modified expected value), the strength of the difference principle (we are more permissive), the thickness of the veil (we think it underdetermines the answer), public reason (we allow more honest acknowledgment of commitments), the focus on distribution alone (production matters too), and the historical universality of Rawlsian liberalism.

  4. Nozick’s libertarian critique points at real problems with pure pattern-based justice, which the framework addresses by recognizing that both process and distribution matter.

  5. Sen’s capability critique is right — the framework’s welfare conception is closer to capabilities than to primary goods, and this matters for the specific content of justice.

  6. The original position is a useful tool but not a decision procedure. It clarifies impartiality and generates insurance arguments but does not yield unique principles from rationality alone.

  7. The framework’s political philosophy is significantly Rawlsian in structure while differing on specific points. The debt is real and the engagement is the most sustained of any rival system.

The next chapter addresses virtue ethics, particularly in its Aristotelian and MacIntyrean forms. We engaged with MacIntyre in Chapter 11; now we engage with virtue ethics as a distinct tradition, showing why the framework draws on it while also departing from its strictest versions.

Chapter 42: Against Virtue Ethics (Without Telos)

“We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” — The Durant paraphrase of Aristotle, preserved in Chapter 11

The Tradition

Virtue ethics is older than utilitarianism or deontology. Its canonical source is Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, but the tradition includes the Stoics, Confucius, Aquinas, and contemporary thinkers like Alasdair MacIntyre, Philippa Foot, Rosalind Hursthouse, and Michael Slote.

The central claim of virtue ethics: the primary question of ethics is not “what should I do?” but “what kind of person should I be?” Virtues (honesty, courage, justice, temperance, practical wisdom, and others) are character traits that constitute a good life. Right action is what a virtuous person would do. Moral theory should focus on developing these character traits rather than on formulating rules or calculating consequences.

This is a serious tradition with deep roots and strong contemporary defenders. It captures something important that both rule-based and consequence-based ethics can miss: the recognition that who we are matters morally, not just what we do or what results we produce.

The framework has absorbed significant elements of virtue ethics — Chapter 11 developed the twelve virtues of rationality, and Chapter 12 addressed moral development as the formation of character. In that sense, the framework is partially virtue-ethical. But we also diverge from pure virtue ethics in important ways, particularly from its Aristotelian and MacIntyrean forms, which depend on teleological claims about human nature that the framework rejects.

This chapter identifies where the framework agrees with virtue ethics, where it disagrees, and why the synthesis it offers is an improvement on the pure virtue-ethical position.

Steel-Manning Aristotelian Virtue Ethics

Aristotle’s argument, compressed: humans have a natural function (ergon), and flourishing (eudaimonia) consists in fulfilling that function well. The Nicomachean Ethics opens with the claim that all human activity aims at some good:

“Every art and every inquiry, and similarly every action and pursuit, is thought to aim at some good; and for this reason the good has rightly been declared to be that at which all things aim.” — Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, I.1 (1094a)

The function of a knife is to cut; a good knife cuts well. The function of a doctor is to heal; a good doctor heals well. The function of a human is to reason well and act in accordance with reason, within the context of a polis (political community). Virtues are the character traits that enable humans to fulfill this function. The result is Aristotle’s definition of the human good:

“The Good of man is the active exercise of his soul’s faculties in conformity with excellence or virtue, or if there be several human excellences or virtues, in conformity with the best and most perfect among them.” — Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, I.7 (1098a)

From this foundational claim, Aristotle derives:

1. Virtues are discovered, not invented. They are features of human flourishing given our nature, not arbitrary choices. Courage, honesty, justice, temperance, and practical wisdom (phronesis) are the virtues because they are what humans need to flourish, not because they happen to be valued in specific cultures.

2. Virtue is habituation. We become virtuous by practicing virtuous acts, not by intellectual acceptance of moral principles. Character is formed through repeated action that eventually becomes second nature.

3. Practical wisdom is central. Unlike rule-based ethics, virtue ethics does not provide algorithms. Instead, it requires practical wisdom — the capacity to perceive what the particular situation calls for. The practically wise person (phronimos) knows how to act rightly in specific circumstances, not because they are applying a rule but because they have developed the perception and judgment that virtue requires.

4. The virtues form a unity. You cannot have courage without practical wisdom (or your “courage” is just recklessness). You cannot have justice without temperance. The virtues reinforce and require each other. A person who is honest but lacks other virtues is not fully virtuous.

5. Eudaimonia is the goal. Not pleasure, not preference satisfaction, not rule-following — the full flourishing of the human being as the kind of creature they are. Eudaimonia is “activity of the soul in accordance with perfect virtue” (NE I.7), and it must be assessed over a complete lifetime — as Aristotle memorably puts it, “one swallow does not make a spring” (I.7, 1098a). This is more objective than utilitarian welfare (because it is grounded in human nature) and more concrete than Kantian principles (because it points at a specific kind of life).

6. Ethics is political. Virtues are developed and exercised in communities. A person in isolation cannot be fully virtuous, because virtues like justice and friendship require others. The polis is the natural context of human flourishing, and the good state is one in which citizens can develop and exercise their virtues.

This is a rich and compelling vision. It captures insights that other moral traditions miss, particularly about character, community, and the role of practical wisdom in navigating complex situations.

MacIntyre’s Contemporary Revival

Alasdair MacIntyre, in After Virtue (1981), mounted the most influential contemporary defense of virtue ethics, and we engaged with his critique in Chapter 11. Briefly:

MacIntyre argued that modern moral philosophy has lost the teleological framework that made classical virtue ethics coherent. Without a shared conception of the human good — without a telos — modern moral discourse becomes incoherent, reducing to emotivism (Stevenson’s view that moral claims are just expressions of preference). The way forward, MacIntyre argued, is to recover virtue ethics embedded in practices (activities with internal standards of excellence), narratives (stories that give unity to a life), and traditions (ongoing communities of inquiry).

MacIntyre’s version is interesting because it does not require a controversial metaphysical telos. Instead, virtues are identified through participation in specific practices — activities like medicine, science, farming, teaching, craftsmanship. Each practice has internal goods that are achieved by excelling in the practice, and the virtues are the character traits that enable this excellence. Justice, courage, honesty, and practical wisdom are virtues in almost every practice because almost every practice requires them.

This is a clever move. It grounds virtues in observable features of human activities rather than in contested metaphysical claims about human nature. MacIntyre gets much of the force of classical virtue ethics while avoiding some of its most contested premises.

But MacIntyre’s position still has commitments that the framework cannot fully accept, particularly the claim that modern moral philosophy is incoherent and that only return to tradition can save it. Chapter 11 addressed this; the framework agrees with part of MacIntyre’s critique while disagreeing with his prescription.

What the Framework Takes from Virtue Ethics

The framework has absorbed significant elements from the virtue tradition:

1. Character matters, not just acts. A person who does the right thing for the wrong reasons, or who has bad character but happens to behave well, is missing something important. The framework’s twelve virtues (Chapter 11) reflect this insight.

2. Habituation is the mechanism of moral development. You become honest by practicing honesty. You become courageous by doing courageous things. Moral development is not primarily intellectual; it is primarily practical. Chapter 12 developed this view.

3. Practical wisdom matters. Rules and principles are insufficient for specific cases. A person navigating real moral situations needs judgment that cannot be fully reduced to algorithms. The framework’s dual-process architecture acknowledges this — Mode A uses rules, but Mode B requires judgment, and virtues are what make the judgment reliable.

4. The unity of virtues. Having one virtue without others produces distorted outcomes. An honest person without tact can be cruel. A courageous person without wisdom can be reckless. The framework’s virtues work as a system, not as a checklist.

5. Virtues are developed in communities. Moral formation happens through participation in communities of practice, not through solitary reflection. The framework acknowledges this (Chapter 12) and incorporates it into the theory of moral development.

6. Flourishing is more than hedonic tone. The framework’s complex value vector (Chapter 3) includes multiple dimensions beyond simple pleasure and pain, reflecting the Aristotelian insight that human flourishing is rich and multifaceted, not reducible to utility calculations.

7. Practices have internal goods. MacIntyre’s insight about practices informs how the framework thinks about meaningful work (Chapter 29) and the structure of institutions (Chapter 18). Activities with internal standards of excellence produce genuine goods that cannot be replaced by purely external rewards.

These are significant debts. The framework is substantially virtue-ethical in its treatment of character, development, and practical wisdom.

Where the Framework Differs

Despite these agreements, the framework diverges from pure virtue ethics on several specific points:

Divergence 1: Telos

Aristotelian virtue ethics depends on the claim that humans have a specific telos — a natural function that defines what flourishing consists in for humans. The framework rejects this claim in its strong form.

The problem: what is the human telos? Aristotle said it was reasoning well in a political community. But different answers produce different virtue theories – reproduction yields one set, knowledge another, pleasure another, service to God another. Aristotle’s answer is one among many, and none can be derived from biology or physics alone.

The framework’s approach: rather than grounding virtues in a contested claim about human telos, ground them in more defensible foundations. Valence (Chapter 3) grounds the basic concern for welfare. Coordination (Book II) grounds the need for character traits that enable cooperation. Epistemic duty (Chapter 2) grounds the need for character traits that enable truth-seeking. These foundations do not require a specific metaphysical telos, yet they generate most of the virtues that the Aristotelian tradition identifies.

This is what we meant earlier by saying the framework’s approach is “virtue ethics without telos.” We keep the virtues; we reject the specific metaphysical story about why they are the virtues. The result is defensible against critics who reject Aristotelian metaphysics while preserving most of the substantive content.

Divergence 2: Decision Procedures

Virtue ethics is famously weak on decision procedures. When you face a specific dilemma, what do you do? The virtue-ethical answer is: “what would the virtuous person do?” But this is not much help if you are trying to figure out what the virtuous person would do, and the theory does not give you much guidance on how to figure it out.

Defenders respond that this is a feature, not a bug – real situations require practical wisdom that cannot be captured in algorithms. There is truth to this. But people in hard situations need more guidance than “use practical wisdom.” They need a framework for thinking through the situation, even if that framework does not determine the answer.

The framework’s dual-process architecture provides this framework. Mode A gives rules for the normal cases. Mode B gives a structured decision procedure (with the five conditions from Chapter 10) for the override cases. Virtues are essential to both — they enable reliable Mode A compliance and reliable Mode B judgment — but the architecture provides guidance that pure virtue ethics lacks.

Divergence 3: The Problem of the Phronimos

Aristotle identifies the practically wise person (phronimos) as the standard of right action: what the phronimos would do is what you should do. But this is circular unless you can identify the phronimos without already knowing what right action is. If you know right action, you can identify the phronimos (the person who consistently does it); if you know the phronimos, you know right action (what they do). But you cannot know both without knowing one first.

Virtue ethicists have various responses to this circle. Some say we identify the phronimos through their track record and reputation, which avoids the circle without fully breaking it. Some say the phronimos is recognized intuitively, which makes the standard vague. Some say the phronimos is an ideal that we can approximate through moral development, which pushes the question back to how moral development works.

The framework’s response: we do not need the phronimos as a standard. We have independent criteria for right action (the framework’s principles from Books I-III) that we can use to evaluate specific choices. These criteria do not replace practical wisdom, but they provide something for practical wisdom to be wise about. A person navigating a hard situation is not merely asking “what would the virtuous person do?” — they are also using the specific tools the framework provides (valence analysis, coordination considerations, rights, etc.) to think through the situation.

Divergence 4: Cultural Embeddedness

Virtue ethics, especially in MacIntyre’s version, emphasizes that virtues are developed in specific traditions and communities. There is truth to this — moral formation does happen in particular contexts, and decontextualized moral reasoning misses something important. But the emphasis can become an argument against universal moral claims, which the framework rejects.

MacIntyre’s version sometimes slides toward the view that moral knowledge is tradition-dependent — that members of different traditions have genuinely different moralities and cannot judge each other. This is close to the moral relativism we rejected in Chapter 40. To the extent that virtue ethics depends on this view, we reject it.

The framework’s position: virtues are developed in traditions, but the traditions can be evaluated against criteria that are not themselves tradition-dependent. Some traditions produce better character than others. Traditions that produce courageous, honest, just people are better than traditions that produce cowardly, deceptive, unjust people. This evaluation is not imperialism; it is recognition that character formation has consequences, and some consequences are better than others by standards that are not merely local.

Divergence 5: The Unity of Virtues Is Overclaimed

Aristotle and some contemporary virtue ethicists argue that the virtues form a strict unity – you cannot have one without all the others. This is too strong. In practice, people have some virtues and lack others. A courageous person may lack patience. An honest person may lack compassion. These are not fake virtues; they are real virtues that happen to exist without some of the others.

The framework’s position: the virtues reinforce each other and work best as a system, but they can exist partially and in isolation. Someone who is working on developing their courage without yet having all the other virtues is still making moral progress, even though their progress is incomplete. The strict unity claim sets a standard that few or no actual people meet, which makes it poorly suited as a practical guide.

Divergence 6: The Role of Rules

Virtue ethics tends to de-emphasize rules in favor of character and judgment. This is valuable as a corrective to rule-fetishism, but it can overshoot. Rules have real value — they are bias-resistant, coordination-enabling, and cognitively efficient (Chapter 9). A purely virtue-based approach misses these benefits.

The framework’s dual-process architecture combines rules and virtues: virtues are the character traits that make reliable rule-following possible, and rules are the practical structure through which virtuous agents act most of the time. This combination is stronger than either pure virtue ethics or pure rule-based ethics alone.

What Virtue Ethics Gets Right (Restated)

Despite these divergences, the framework is substantially indebted to virtue ethics. It is worth stating the debts clearly:

1. The primacy of character. Moral philosophy that focuses on acts without addressing character is incomplete. The framework agrees.

2. The importance of habituation. Moral development is primarily practical, not primarily intellectual. The framework agrees.

3. Practical wisdom as irreducible. No algorithm can replace judgment in specific cases. The framework agrees.

4. Community and practice as formative contexts. Moral formation happens in communities, through participation in practices. The framework agrees.

5. Multidimensional flourishing. Welfare is not reducible to a single metric. The framework’s value vector reflects this.

6. The internal goods of activities. MacIntyre’s insight about practices is important for understanding meaningful work and institutional structure. The framework uses it.

7. The role of emotion in moral perception. Virtues involve feeling rightly, not just acting rightly. A person who gives to charity while resenting every dollar is missing something that a person who gives gladly is not. The framework’s account of moral development (Chapter 12) incorporates this.

These are large debts. The framework is what you might call “character-informed consequentialism plus rules” — but the “character-informed” part is doing a lot of work, and it comes mostly from the virtue tradition.

The Contemporary Convergence

Contemporary virtue ethicists (Hursthouse, Slote, Swanton, and others) have developed versions of virtue ethics that are more flexible than pure Aristotelianism and more compatible with other moral traditions. They emphasize:

  • Virtues as character traits that promote human flourishing, without necessarily committing to a strong telos.
  • Right action as what the virtuous person would do, supplemented by explicit rules and principles where virtues alone are underdetermining.
  • The role of moral emotions and perceptions, not just abstract principles.
  • The developmental and community contexts in which virtues are formed.

This contemporary virtue ethics is closer to the framework than classical Aristotelianism. If you asked a contemporary virtue ethicist what their view implies in specific cases, their answers would often align with the framework’s. The disagreements are about which considerations are primary and how to structure the theoretical apparatus, not about what to do in specific situations.

The Verdict

The framework is significantly virtue-ethical in its treatment of character, habituation, practical wisdom, and community. But it is not pure virtue ethics. It differs on:

  • The telos question: rejecting strong metaphysical claims about human nature while preserving the role of virtues.
  • Decision procedures: providing the dual-process architecture as guidance where pure virtue ethics leaves agents unaided.
  • The phronimos standard: providing independent criteria for right action rather than circularly defining them through the virtuous agent.
  • Cultural embeddedness: rejecting the slide toward relativism while acknowledging the role of traditions in moral formation.
  • The unity of virtues: allowing partial virtues rather than insisting on all-or-nothing.
  • The role of rules: combining rule-based and virtue-based approaches rather than privileging either.

The result is a position that takes seriously what virtue ethics gets right (character, development, practical wisdom, community) while avoiding its weaknesses (circularity, weak decision guidance, dependence on contested metaphysics, potential slide toward relativism).

As with Rawls and with utilitarianism, the framework’s engagement with virtue ethics is substantive rather than dismissive. The tradition has real insights, and we have absorbed them. The disagreements are specific and defensible. A person who accepts virtue ethics as a starting point and then considers the framework’s specific arguments would find much to agree with, and the remaining disagreements would be about particular points rather than about the whole approach.

Summary

  1. Virtue ethics focuses on character traits (virtues) that constitute a good life, drawing on Aristotle, MacIntyre, and contemporary thinkers.

  2. Aristotle’s strengths include grounding virtues in human flourishing, the role of habituation, practical wisdom, the unity of virtues, eudaimonia as the goal, and the political context of ethics.

  3. The framework absorbs the primacy of character, the importance of habituation, practical wisdom as irreducible, community and practice as formative contexts, multidimensional flourishing, and the moral role of emotions.

  4. The framework differs on the telos (we reject strong metaphysical claims about human nature), decision procedures (we provide the dual-process architecture), the phronimos standard (we provide independent criteria), cultural embeddedness (we reject the slide toward relativism), the unity of virtues (we allow partial virtues), and the role of rules (we combine rules with virtues).

  5. Contemporary virtue ethicists have developed positions closer to the framework than pure Aristotelianism. Convergence from multiple directions strengthens confidence in the framework.

  6. The verdict: the framework is significantly virtue-ethical but not purely so. The debts are real and the disagreements are specific rather than fundamental.

The next chapter addresses a very different tradition: Marxist and critical theory ethics. These traditions are often dismissed by liberal philosophers but contain insights that the framework must engage with seriously.

Chapter 43: Against Marxist and Critical Theory Ethics

“The philosophers have only interpreted the world in various ways; the point, however, is to change it.” — Karl Marx, Theses on Feuerbach

The Challenge

Marxism is often dismissed by mainstream moral philosophy, especially in the English-speaking world, where it is associated with twentieth-century political disasters. This dismissal is a mistake. Marx himself was a serious thinker whose analysis of capitalism, alienation, exploitation, and ideology contains insights that any comprehensive moral theory should engage with. The same applies to the broader tradition of Critical Theory (Frankfurt School, Marcuse, Habermas) and to contemporary critical traditions.

These traditions share several commitments:

  1. Material conditions shape consciousness. How people think about ethics, politics, and justice is influenced (not determined, but shaped) by their position in material and social structures.

  2. Ideology obscures reality. Dominant ideas in a society often serve the interests of the dominant group, while appearing to be neutral truths. Critical analysis exposes these ideas as ideology.

  3. Power is pervasive. Moral and political questions cannot be separated from questions of power — who has it, how it is exercised, who benefits, who is harmed.

  4. Structures matter more than individual intentions. Systems produce outcomes that no individual participant intended and may not even be aware of. Focusing on individual morality while ignoring structural dynamics is incomplete.

  5. Theory should be practical. The point of analysis is not just to understand the world but to change it. Theory divorced from practice is impoverished.

The framework must engage with these claims. Some of them, we already endorse. Others, we reject or modify. This chapter works through the engagement carefully, because the stakes are high — if the critical traditions are right about things the framework misses, the framework is incomplete.

Steel-Manning Marx

Marx’s theoretical edifice is too large to summarize fully, but the core claims that bear on ethics include:

1. Capitalism is exploitative. Under capitalism, workers produce more value than they receive in wages. The difference (surplus value) is appropriated by capitalists who did not produce it. This exploitation is structural, not accidental — it is how capitalism works, not a distortion of how it should work. Reform that leaves the structure intact cannot eliminate exploitation.

2. Capitalism alienates workers. Workers in capitalist production are separated from the products of their labor (which belong to others), from their own creative capacities (which are sold as labor power), from other workers (who become competitors for jobs), and from their own human potential (which is reduced to what the market will pay for). Alienation is not psychological malaise but a structural feature of capitalist production.

3. Ideology serves class interests. The dominant ideas in a capitalist society — liberal rights, market efficiency, meritocracy, individual responsibility — are not neutral. They are the ideas that serve the interests of the owning class by legitimating the existing order and obscuring its injustices. Critical analysis exposes this.

4. History has direction. Societies develop through predictable stages driven by contradictions in their economic structures. Capitalism will generate crises that will eventually produce its own supersession by a different mode of production (Marx thought socialism, then communism). This historical analysis is not mere prediction; it is the basis for understanding current conditions and strategy.

5. Class struggle is the motor of change. The conflicts between those who own means of production and those who work them (along with related conflicts) are what drive historical change. Political action that ignores class dynamics misses the fundamental force shaping society.

6. Morality is (partly) ideology. Moral claims are not purely about objective right and wrong; they reflect the interests and perspectives of particular classes. “Bourgeois morality” — with its emphasis on private property, individual responsibility, and liberal rights — is the morality that serves capitalist interests, presented as universal ethics.

7. The goal is human emancipation. Beyond fixing specific injustices, the Marxist project aims at liberating humans from conditions that distort their development and prevent their full flourishing. Even in his earliest writings, Marx framed freedom as constitutive of the human rather than optional:

“Freedom is so much the essence of man that even its opponents implement it while combating its reality; they want to appropriate for themselves as a most precious ornament what they have rejected as an ornament of human nature.” — Karl Marx, “Debates on Freedom of the Press” (1842), Collected Works Vol. 1

And his question about whether freedom is “a privilege of particular individuals or whether it is a privilege of the human mind” — whether rights are for the few or for all — captures the universalist impulse that drives the tradition from its earliest days through the mature critique of Capital.

This is a powerful vision. It identifies real problems, offers a systematic account of their causes, and points toward a normative ideal that is appealing even if specific prescriptions are questionable.

What Marx Gets Right

Several Marxist insights are, in the framework’s view, correct:

1. Structural analysis is essential. You cannot understand moral and political problems by looking only at individual choices. Structures — economic arrangements, institutional designs, power relationships — shape what choices are available, what incentives operate, and what outcomes occur. The framework’s coordination analysis (Book II) and mechanism design approach (Chapter 8) agree with this. We just call it different things.

2. Ideology is real. Dominant ideas often serve dominant interests while appearing neutral. The framework has its own version of this insight in Chapter 2 (motivated reasoning, Chapter 2’s warnings about self-serving reasoning) and Chapter 4 (the Alien God’s influence on moral intuitions). Marx was ahead of much of his time in identifying this phenomenon.

3. Exploitation is a real category. When one person produces value that another appropriates without compensation or consent, something morally significant is happening. The framework agrees that this can be wrong, even in voluntary transactions when the voluntariness is undermined by power asymmetries (Chapter 26 discussed this in the context of exchange).

4. Alienation captures something real. People can be disconnected from their work, from their capacities, from their communities, from themselves. The framework’s treatment of meaningful work (Chapter 29) and human flourishing (Chapter 15) acknowledges this. Marx identified it clearly and named it usefully.

5. Material conditions matter. What people think and how they live is heavily influenced by their economic circumstances. Moral theory that ignores material conditions is airy and disconnected from reality. The framework’s political and economic chapters take material conditions seriously.

6. Power must be analyzed. Who has power, how it is exercised, who benefits, who is harmed — these questions are central to political and moral analysis. Frameworks that ignore power relations are incomplete. The framework’s engagement with institutional design, rights, and the state all involve power analysis.

7. Theory should inform practice. The point of moral and political analysis is not just intellectual understanding but to affect how people live and how societies are organized. The framework agrees — we have been applying theory to practice throughout Books IV-VII.

These are substantial concessions. The framework takes Marxist insights seriously and incorporates many of them. The disagreements are about what to do with these insights, not about whether they are valid.

Where the Framework Disagrees with Marx

Despite the agreements, the framework differs from Marxism on several specific points:

Disagreement 1: The Labor Theory of Value

Marx’s economic analysis rests on the labor theory of value — the claim that the value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labor time required to produce it. From this, the theory of surplus value and exploitation follows. If labor is the source of value, and workers receive less than the value they produce, they are being exploited.

The problem: modern economics has largely rejected the labor theory of value. Value is better understood as determined by marginal utility and scarcity. Labor is one input among several (capital, land, entrepreneurship, technology, natural resources), and the marginal revolution (Menger, Jevons, Walras) provided a more accurate account of how prices form.

This matters because much of Marx’s moral analysis depends on the labor theory. If labor is not the sole source of value, then the extraction of “surplus value” is not the theft it appears to be. Capitalists, entrepreneurs, and workers all contribute to value, and each can reasonably claim some share of the result.

The framework’s response: exploitation is a real category, but it should be redefined. Exploitation, in the framework’s usage, is when one party extracts value from another through coercion, fraud, or severe power asymmetries that undermine genuine consent. This happens in some employment relationships, but not in all. A voluntary exchange between a worker and an employer, under conditions of reasonable labor markets with multiple employers and some worker mobility, is not exploitation in the problematic sense. An exchange under conditions of severe power asymmetry (monopsony, coercion, desperation) might be.

This is a weaker claim than Marx’s, but it is more defensible empirically. And it points at specific cases where intervention is warranted without condemning all capitalist production as inherently exploitative.

Disagreement 2: Historical Materialism and Prediction

Marx’s predictions about historical development – the intensification of class struggle, the immiseration of workers, capitalism’s replacement by socialism – have mostly not come true. Capitalism has proven more adaptive than Marx expected. Workers in wealthy capitalist countries are generally better off than their ancestors. Class struggle has been moderated by labor laws, welfare states, and the expansion of the middle class. Where the transition to socialism was attempted, it produced economic failure and authoritarianism.

This does not refute everything Marx said, but it refutes his specific historical predictions, suggesting that the theoretical machinery generating them has problems.

The framework’s response: structural analysis is valuable, but historical prediction is harder than Marx thought. Societies evolve in ways that depend on many variables, and linear predictions from current structures to future outcomes are unreliable. The framework uses structural analysis as a tool for understanding specific problems, not as the basis for sweeping predictions about the direction of history.

Disagreement 3: The Critique of Morality Goes Too Far

Marx argued that morality is partly ideology, serving the interests of dominant classes. This is true in part. But Marx sometimes extended the claim to a general skepticism about moral reasoning, treating moral claims as mere reflections of class position and material interests.

The framework’s response: ideology is a real phenomenon, but it does not discredit all moral reasoning. Some moral claims are objective — grounded in valence and coordination considerations that are not reducible to class interests. Some moral claims are ideology — serving particular interests while claiming universality. The skill is to distinguish the two, which requires moral reasoning that does not collapse into pure critique.

If Marx were right that all moral reasoning is ideology, then his own moral claims (about exploitation, alienation, emancipation) would also be ideology, and the theory would be self-undermining. Marx himself was not entirely consistent on this; he sometimes wrote as if his critique provided access to genuine moral truth that bourgeois morality obscured. The framework is more consistent: moral reasoning can track genuine features of reality, while also being subject to distortion by interest and ideology.

Disagreement 4: Revolution as Solution

Marx argued that the structural problems of capitalism cannot be solved by reform — the system must be replaced. Revolution is the mechanism. This commits Marxism to radical political action and, in the 20th century implementation, to violent seizure of state power.

The framework rejects this prescription on several grounds:

1. Historical track record. Revolutions aiming at the replacement of capitalism with socialism have typically produced regimes that were worse than what they replaced. The Soviet Union, Mao’s China, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge, Venezuela in recent decades. This is not random misfortune; it reflects something about the difficulty of replacing complex systems with untested alternatives and the susceptibility of revolutionary movements to authoritarian capture.

2. Error-correction. The framework’s commitment to error-correction primacy (Chapter 18) suggests that gradual reform is preferable to revolutionary replacement. Reforms can be tested, adjusted, and reversed if they fail. Revolutions produce sudden transitions that cannot easily be reversed, and when they fail, the costs are enormous.

3. Reformist alternatives have worked. Social democracy — reformed capitalism with strong welfare states and labor protections — has produced outcomes significantly better than both pure capitalism and revolutionary socialism. The Nordic countries, while not perfect, demonstrate that reformist paths can achieve many of the goods that revolutionary Marxism aimed at.

4. The assumption of radical replacement is flawed. Marx assumed that capitalism could be replaced with a wholly different system that would avoid its pathologies without introducing new ones. This is speculative. The framework is more cautious: gradual change within a functioning system is safer than radical replacement, and specific reforms can address specific problems without requiring wholesale system change.

This is not a defense of the status quo. The framework supports significant reforms — Chapter 28 on the safety net, Chapter 29 on labor, Chapter 30 on fiscal policy, Chapter 27 on externalities all argue for substantial changes. But reform rather than revolution is the framework’s preferred mechanism, and the historical evidence supports this preference.

Disagreement 5: Class as the Primary Category

Marx treated class — defined by relationship to the means of production — as the primary social category. Other divisions (race, sex, nationality, religion) were secondary, reducible to class in the last analysis.

This is not supported by the evidence. Class matters, but so do other divisions, and they are not reducible to class. Sex-based oppression exists in both capitalist and non-capitalist societies. Racial hierarchies are not mere functions of class positions. Religious conflicts have dynamics independent of economics. The irreducibility of these divisions is a significant problem for classical Marxism.

Contemporary critical theorists have addressed this by expanding the categories — intersectionality, critical race theory, feminist critique, postcolonial analysis. These developments are genuine improvements on classical Marxism’s reductionism. But they also change the theory significantly, and the result is no longer simply Marxism — it is a broader critical tradition that includes Marxism as one component.

The framework’s response: multiple forms of power and oppression exist, and the specific analysis depends on the specific case. Economic class is one important dimension. Race is another. Sex is another. Nationality is another. These interact in complex ways, and no single category is primary across all situations. The framework uses the analytical tools relevant to specific questions rather than privileging one category over others.

Critical Theory and Its Successors

The Frankfurt School (Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, Habermas) developed Marxist insights in new directions, often engaging with questions Marx himself did not address in depth: culture, psychology, communication, reason, and the Enlightenment project.

Some of their insights the framework endorses:

1. Instrumental reason is dangerous when unchecked. Pure means-ends rationality, applied to everything, can produce monstrous outcomes — efficient extermination camps, optimized surveillance states, maximized quarterly profits at the expense of everything else. Reason must be accompanied by values it does not itself generate. The framework agrees (Chapter 2 explicitly distinguishes epistemic rationality from moral foundations).

2. Mass culture can produce conformity and passivity. When cultural production is dominated by a small number of corporations optimizing for engagement, the result can be cultural impoverishment. The framework’s treatment of the digital environment (Chapter 35) addresses related concerns.

3. Language shapes thought. How we talk about things affects how we think about them. Ideological framings embedded in language influence how we reason. Critical analysis of language is a legitimate tool, even if it is sometimes overused.

4. Communicative rationality matters (Habermas). The conditions under which genuine dialogue can occur — equality of speakers, absence of coercion, mutual recognition — are morally and politically important. The framework’s treatment of the epistemic commons (Chapter 21) and democratic deliberation (Chapter 20) reflects related concerns.

Contemporary critical traditions (critical race theory, feminist critical theory, postcolonial theory, queer theory) have extended these insights to specific forms of oppression. The framework engages with these as it does with classical Marxism — taking the insights seriously, questioning the specific claims where they seem overstated, and integrating what works with the broader framework.

The most valuable contributions of contemporary critical traditions:

  • Attention to specific historical and structural injustices that liberal frameworks sometimes overlook.
  • Centering the perspectives of the marginalized, whose experiences provide evidence that dominant groups often lack.
  • Analysis of how neutral-sounding institutions can produce unequal outcomes, even in the absence of explicit discrimination.
  • Recognition that formal equality is insufficient if substantive inequalities persist.
  • Critique of the universalist pretenses of particular traditions, reminding us that all frameworks are situated.

The framework absorbs these insights while resisting some of the more radical claims of contemporary critical theory:

  • We do not accept that all social categories are purely constructed with no basis in reality.
  • We do not accept that power analysis replaces all other forms of moral analysis.
  • We do not accept that truth is purely a function of power (this would self-refute like the relativism we rejected in Chapter 40).
  • We do not accept that liberal institutions are fundamentally unreformable and must be replaced.
  • We do not accept that rigorous reasoning is itself a form of oppression.

The framework is not post-modern, not purely structural, and not anti-liberal. It is liberal in the broad sense (committed to individual rights, democratic institutions, open discourse, and the possibility of reform) while being informed by the critical insights about how these institutions can produce unjust outcomes when left unchecked.

What the Framework Owes the Critical Traditions

Putting the engagement together, the framework owes specific debts to Marxism and critical theory:

1. The analysis of structural injustice — the recognition that bad outcomes can be produced by systems rather than by individual malice, and that fixing them requires structural change rather than moral exhortation.

2. The concept of ideology — the awareness that dominant ideas can serve dominant interests while appearing neutral. The framework’s epistemic humility (Chapter 2) has Marxist ancestry.

3. Attention to exploitation and power asymmetries — even when we narrow the definition of exploitation, the underlying concern is legitimate and important.

4. The insight that material conditions shape consciousness — what people think is not independent of how they live, and serious moral philosophy must account for this.

5. Analysis of alienation and meaningful work — the framework’s treatment of labor and flourishing draws on this.

6. The importance of specific historical injustices — slavery, colonialism, patriarchy, discrimination. These shaped current conditions and cannot be dismissed as “past” issues.

7. The reminder that theory should serve practice — moral philosophy divorced from how people actually live is impoverished.

8. The critique of liberal self-satisfaction — liberal societies have real achievements but also real failures, and the critical tradition keeps the failures visible.

These are substantial debts. The framework is not “anti-Marxist” in the sense of dismissing everything Marxists said. It is selectively engaged, agreeing with some Marxist insights, modifying others, and rejecting some specific claims.

The Practical Upshot

What does this chapter imply for how the framework actually operates?

1. Economic and political analysis should include structural and power considerations. Pure individual-choice analysis misses too much. When analyzing specific situations, ask: who has power here? How is it exercised? Who benefits? Who bears costs? These questions should be routine, not optional.

2. Exploitation, even narrowly defined, is a real category and warrants attention. Workers facing monopsonistic employers, debtors facing usurious lenders, citizens facing captured regulators — these are situations where power asymmetries can produce unjust outcomes even in “voluntary” transactions.

3. Structural reform is legitimate and sometimes necessary. Not everything can be fixed by individual moral choices or by small adjustments within existing structures. Some problems require institutional change. The framework’s policy analysis (Chapter 24) supports this.

4. Beware of ideology, including your own. Your moral and political views are partly shaped by your interests and position. Take this seriously. Engage with critics whose perspectives differ from yours. Notice when your conclusions conveniently align with your interests.

5. Don’t dismiss critiques that come from unfashionable sources. Marxists have real insights even when their political projects have failed. Critical theorists have real insights even when their rhetoric is sometimes excessive. Engagement with hostile critics is often more valuable than engagement with friendly ones.

6. Reform, not revolution. The framework commits to gradual, error-correcting change rather than radical replacement. This commits us to patience and to working within existing institutions, while also insisting that the institutions must change when they are producing unjust outcomes.

Summary

  1. Marxism and critical theory have been dismissed too easily by mainstream moral philosophy. The traditions contain real insights.

  2. Marx’s core claims include exploitation, alienation, ideology, historical materialism, class struggle, and human emancipation. Some are valuable; some are problematic.

  3. The framework agrees on structural analysis, ideology critique, the reality of exploitation (narrowly defined), the importance of alienation, material conditions, power analysis, and practice-oriented theory.

  4. The framework disagrees on the labor theory of value (rejected), historical predictions (mostly failed), the scope of the critique of morality (too broad), revolution as solution (bad track record), and class as the primary category (not supported by evidence).

  5. The Frankfurt School and contemporary critical theory extended Marx’s insights in valuable directions while adding specific critiques of instrumental reason, mass culture, language, and specific forms of oppression.

  6. The framework absorbs attention to structural injustice, ideology, exploitation, material conditions, historical injustices, and the limits of liberal self-satisfaction.

  7. The framework rejects radical social constructionism, the reduction of truth to power, wholesale anti-liberalism, and the rejection of rigorous reasoning as oppression.

  8. The practical upshot: include structural and power analysis in moral reasoning, take critique seriously including from unfashionable sources, commit to reform rather than revolution, beware of your own ideological biases.

The next chapter addresses natural law theory — the tradition running through Aquinas, Catholic moral philosophy, and contemporary natural law theorists. This is the last of the major rival systems to engage before we turn to non-Western traditions.

Chapter 44: Against Natural Law Theory

“The light of natural reason, whereby we discern what is good and what is evil, which is the function of the natural law, is nothing else than an imprint on us of the Divine light.” — Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, I-II, Q.91, A.2

The Rival

Natural Law Theory is one of the oldest and most institutionally consequential moral frameworks in Western thought. It holds that moral truths are not invented by human beings, not revealed by sporadic divine commands, and not constructed from coordination pressures — they are written into the structure of reality itself, specifically into the nature of the things that morality concerns. To know what is good for a human being, you look at what a human being is. To know what is right, you look at what human flourishing consists in, which is fixed by human nature, which is fixed by the intelligent ordering of the cosmos.

This framework has powerful adherents. The Thomistic synthesis built by Aquinas in the thirteenth century remains the official moral theology of the Roman Catholic Church and shapes the moral reasoning of over a billion people. In the twentieth century, John Finnis, Germain Grisez, and Robert George developed “new natural law theory,” which detaches the core arguments from explicit Aristotelian metaphysics and defends them in terms accessible to secular readers. Natural law undergirds much of international human rights law, the Nuremberg prosecutions (which appealed to a law higher than positive German law), and serious strands of contemporary jurisprudence.

It is the most sophisticated non-theistic-in-practice alternative to our framework: theistic in its foundations but argued at length in terms of reason, nature, and flourishing rather than scriptural commands. For this reason it demands a different kind of engagement than Chapter 37’s treatment of Divine Command Theory. Natural law is not “God said so” — it is “reason, reflecting on what human beings are, discovers what human beings should do.” That is a serious claim.

This chapter steel-mans natural law in both its Thomistic and new natural law forms, identifies what the framework owes it (which is considerable), and then shows where it breaks down.

Steel-Manning Natural Law: The Thomistic Version

Aquinas’s treatment in the Summa Theologica (Prima Secundae, Questions 90–97) is the canonical statement. The structure is precise:

Law is ordered reason. Aquinas defines law as “an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated” (Q.90, A.4). This is not arbitrary will — divine or human — but reason directed to the good of those subject to the law. A law that violates this definition is not merely a bad law; it is not genuinely a law at all. “Lex iniusta non est lex” — an unjust law is no law.

Natural law is eternal law reflected in rational creatures. Behind natural law stands eternal law: God’s own reason, which orders all of creation toward its ends. Irrational creatures participate in eternal law by their natural operations (fire burns, water flows, plants grow). Rational creatures participate in a distinctive way — by understanding the order they are part of and freely directing themselves toward their end. This rational participation in eternal law is the natural law. As Aquinas puts it, “the natural law is promulgated by the very fact that God instilled it into man’s mind so as to be known by him naturally” (Q.90, A.4, ad 1).

The first precept is good is to be done. Aquinas holds that practical reason has first principles analogous to the first principles of theoretical reason. The first indemonstrable principle of theoretical reason is the law of non-contradiction. The first precept of practical reason is this:

“Good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. All other precepts of the natural law are based upon this.” — Aquinas, Summa Theologica, I-II, Q.94, A.2

This is not derived. It is self-evident to practical reason. Just as no one can coherently deny the law of non-contradiction (because denial presupposes it), no one can coherently act without treating some end as good and pursuing it. “Every agent acts for an end under the aspect of good.”

Specific precepts derive from natural inclinations. From the first precept, more specific content comes via reflection on the natural inclinations of the human being. Aquinas distinguishes three levels:

  1. Inclinations shared with all substances: self-preservation. “Whatever is a means of preserving human life, and of warding off its obstacles, belongs to the natural law.”
  2. Inclinations shared with other animals: reproduction and education of offspring. “Those things are said to belong to the natural law which nature has taught to all animals, such as sexual intercourse, education of offspring and so forth.”
  3. Inclinations proper to human rational nature: “to know the truth about God, and to live in society; and in this respect, whatever pertains to this inclination belongs to the natural law; for instance, to shun ignorance, to avoid offending those among whom one has to live, and other such things.”

Moral reasoning, on this picture, is the articulation of what these inclinations, understood rightly, require. You discover your duties by understanding your nature.

Natural law is universal and (mostly) unchangeable. Because natural law is grounded in what human beings are, and human nature does not change, the natural law is the same for all human beings across all times and places (Q.94, A.4). Aquinas allows for some variation at the level of secondary principles (because particular circumstances can affect how a principle applies) but not at the level of the first precept and its most proximate specifications.

Human law should be derived from natural law. Positive law — the actual legal enactments of human communities — is legitimate only when it is consistent with natural law. Laws contrary to the natural law are “acts of violence rather than laws” (Q.96, A.4). This is not a recipe for disobedience in every case (Aquinas is cautious about when one must actively disobey) but it establishes a standard above positive law by which positive law can be judged.

This framework has features that should be noted before critique. It is rational rather than voluntarist – moral truths are discovered by reason, not commanded by will. It is teleological – things have ends built into them, and moral reasoning reflects on those ends. It is objective, universal, and integrated with politics and law – moral theory grounds legal theory, which grounds institutional practice.

Steel-Manning Natural Law: The New Natural Law Version

The Thomistic version depends on metaphysical commitments (teleological biology, eternal law, rational theism) that many contemporary readers do not share. Finnis and Grisez’s “new natural law theory,” beginning with Finnis’s Natural Law and Natural Rights (1980), reformulates the core argument without requiring those commitments.

Basic goods. Finnis argues that reflection on human action reveals a set of basic goods — things that are intelligibly valuable as ends in themselves, not merely as means to something else. His list, with some variation over the years: life (including health and bodily integrity), knowledge (truth), play, aesthetic experience, sociability (friendship), practical reasonableness, and religion (or, in later versions, harmony with a transcendent source of meaning). These are not the same as felt desires; they are the ends that make desires intelligible.

Incommensurability. The basic goods are irreducibly plural. You cannot trade off knowledge against friendship on a common scale, because they are different kinds of good. This is a critical move: it blocks the utilitarian strategy of reducing everything to one metric and maximizing.

Practical reasonableness. Given the basic goods, how should one act? Finnis identifies nine “requirements of practical reasonableness”: have a coherent life plan; no arbitrary preference among values; no arbitrary preference among persons; detachment from any one project; commitment to one’s commitments; efficiency within reason; respect for every basic value in every act (the famous “never directly attack a basic good” principle); respect for the common good; follow your conscience.

Moral absolutes. The seventh requirement — “never directly attack a basic good” — generates absolute prohibitions. You may not directly kill an innocent person even to save more people. You may not lie even when lying would prevent great harm. You may not destroy a basic good in order to promote more of it or more of another good. This is close to Kantian deontology but grounded in the structure of the goods themselves rather than in the form of rational will.

Natural rights. Rights are the reverse side of duties generated by practical reasonableness: because you must not directly attack the basic good of life in another, each person has a right not to be so attacked. Natural law thereby generates natural rights without needing a separate grounding theory.

This framework is more accessible to secular readers than the Thomistic original, but its core claims are the same: moral truths are objective features of reality discovered by practical reason reflecting on what is good for human beings.

What the Framework Owes to Natural Law

Natural law is genuinely insightful in several ways the framework must acknowledge.

1. The teleological intuition is partly right. The framework’s valence realism (Chapter 3) says conscious experience has intrinsic valence — suffering is genuinely bad and flourishing is genuinely good. This is a more modest claim than Aquinas’s full teleology (we do not claim that hearts exist for the sake of pumping blood in a morally relevant sense), but it captures the core of the natural law intuition: there are facts about what is good for conscious beings, and those facts are not invented by preference.

2. Practical reason has first principles. The framework agrees that moral reasoning has starting points that cannot be further derived. Our starting points are the valence axiom (suffering matters) and the epistemic duty (truth-seeking is obligatory). These play a role very similar to Aquinas’s first precept of practical reason. The framework differs in what the starting points are, but not in the structural claim that some starting points are needed.

3. Moral truths are objective in a relevant sense. The framework is not relativist. It holds that some moral systems work better than others, that some arrangements produce more suffering and less flourishing, that these are matters of fact rather than taste. This is not the full Thomistic metaphysical objectivism, but it shares the insistence that morality is not merely subjective.

4. Flourishing is the right category. The framework’s complex value vector (hedonic tone, autonomy, competence, connection, understanding, meaning — Chapter 3) is a cousin of the natural law theorist’s basic goods. We are not eudaimonists in the Aristotelian sense, but we agree that human well-being is multidimensional and not reducible to hedonic tone alone. This is a major point of contact with natural law.

5. Law and morality are not separate domains. The framework agrees with Aquinas that the legitimacy of positive law depends on its conformity with moral standards. Our political philosophy (Chapters 17–24) treats institutions as evaluable by their contribution to flourishing and their fit with coordination requirements, not as self-justifying by virtue of being enacted. An unjust law is, in our framework as in Aquinas’s, a failure of law — though we would describe the failure in different terms.

6. There are absolute prohibitions. The framework’s Mode A / Mode B architecture (Chapters 9–10) preserves many of the strong rules that Aquinas and Finnis defend absolutely. We do not treat any rule as metaphysically unbreakable, but we set the override threshold so high that in practice the strongest rules function much as natural law absolutes do. The difference is structural (we have an articulated override mechanism) but the extensional overlap is significant.

This is a substantial debt. Natural law is not a rival we dismiss; it is a rival we have learned from. The specific places where we diverge are therefore worth stating carefully.

Where the Framework Disagrees

Disagreement 1: The Teleological Premise Is Too Strong

Natural law, in its Thomistic form, depends on an Aristotelian teleological biology: things have intrinsic ends (telē) built into what they are, and morality consists in acting in accordance with those ends. The heart exists for pumping blood; the eye exists for seeing; the human being exists for rational participation in the divine order.

Modern biology tells a different story. Organs and traits exist because they were selected for by differential reproduction over evolutionary time. There is no telos in the strong Aristotelian sense – no purpose built into the structure of things, only the residue of past selection pressures (see Chapter 4). The heart’s “function” is a historical fact about what it was selected for, not a metaphysical fact about what it is ordered to.

This matters because natural law’s ability to generate specific moral content depends on reading ends off nature. If the ends are not there in the strong sense, the content cannot be read off. Finnis’s move to “basic goods” is an attempt to rescue the framework by relocating the ends — not in biology but in what practical reason recognizes as intelligibly valuable. But this is a significant retreat: it gives up the claim that ends are written into the nature of things and admits that the goods are identified by reflection on action. Once you make that concession, the framework looks much less like “reading nature” and much more like the kind of reflective equilibrium that any contemporary moral theorist engages in.

The framework’s response: accept the valence realism but reject the strong teleology. Suffering and flourishing are genuine features of conscious experience; they are not projected onto neutral facts. But the move from “suffering is bad” to “here are the specific things you must do” is not a reading of natural ends. It is a reflective construction informed by valence, coordination, and epistemic constraints. The construction is not arbitrary — it is disciplined by the objective features of reality — but it is construction, not decipherment.

Disagreement 2: The “Naturalistic Fallacy” Lands Harder Than Natural Law Admits

Hume’s worry that you cannot derive ought from is, and G. E. Moore’s related “naturalistic fallacy,” are aimed at positions like natural law. The natural law theorist says: human beings have a natural inclination to self-preservation, therefore they ought to preserve themselves. But the “therefore” carries a normative weight that the premise does not obviously supply. Why should natural inclinations be morally authoritative? What argument bridges the descriptive fact that humans tend to self-preserve and the normative conclusion that they should?

Aquinas’s answer is that the inclinations are themselves instances of rational participation in eternal law — that is, the descriptive facts are already morally loaded because they are part of God’s ordering of creation. This answer is available if you accept the theistic metaphysics, but it reintroduces the dependence on God that Finnis is trying to avoid. Finnis’s answer is that the basic goods are recognized as goods by practical reason itself, without needing a further bridge — the recognition is immediate. But critics have argued persuasively that this just relocates the problem: how do we know that practical reason’s recognitions track something real, rather than reporting the preferences of creatures like us?

The framework’s response: the valence axiom handles the bridge more honestly than natural law does. We admit up front that a normative claim is being asserted (suffering matters) and defend it on the grounds that denying it is performatively incoherent and that every moral system requires at least one such axiom. Natural law smuggles the normative content in by calling inclinations “natural” and then treating “natural” as already normative. Our version is more transparent about where the normativity enters.

Disagreement 3: The Content-Generation Problem

A moral framework has to actually tell you what to do in specific cases. Natural law has a long track record of generating specific content, and much of this content is disputable in ways that suggest the method is less reliable than its defenders claim.

Consider the natural law tradition’s positions on sexuality. From the premise that the sexual faculty has a natural purpose (procreation and unitive love within marriage), the tradition derives absolute prohibitions on contraception, masturbation, same-sex sexual activity, and extramarital sex – taught as exceptionless moral norms grounded in the structure of the natural faculty.

But look at the actual inferential chain. Sexual activity serves multiple functions across cultures: reproduction, pleasure, pair-bonding, social cohesion, play, expression, consolation, signaling. Natural law’s move is to privilege one of these functions (reproduction + marital union) as the natural purpose and treat deviations as morally disordered. This privileging is a choice, not an observation. The faculty is multifunctional in fact. The decision to make one function normatively privileged is an extra step that natural law’s method does not justify from inside itself.

Similar issues arise with the tradition’s positions on lying (all lies forbidden, even to save innocent life), on self-defense (complex doctrine of double effect to license killing in self-defense), on capital punishment (varies by period), on usury (once absolutely forbidden, now permitted under new accounts). The content generated by the method has shifted over time in ways that suggest what is actually happening is moral reflection informed by a changing set of inputs — not the direct reading of an unchanging nature.

The framework’s response: acknowledge that moral content is generated through reflective reasoning informed by empirical and theoretical considerations, rather than by reading nature. Our method is fallibilist — it expects to update and it has an explicit mechanism (the Position Registry, Chapter 1) for tracking updates. Natural law’s self-presentation as reading unchanging truths makes it harder for the tradition to acknowledge and learn from its own shifts.

Disagreement 4: The Absolutism Problem

New natural law theory generates absolute prohibitions via its “never directly attack a basic good” principle. You may never intend the death of an innocent person, even to save many. This produces the famous cases where natural law theorists hold that you must not, for example, push a fat man onto trolley tracks to save five others, even if the math is clear.

The framework takes these intuitions seriously — they motivate the dual-process architecture in Chapters 9–10. But we do not handle them by making the rules metaphysically absolute. We handle them by setting a very high override threshold, justified by the game-theoretic reasons rules need to be pre-committed (Chapters 7–9). In practice, the framework reaches the same conclusion as the natural law theorist in the trolley case (do not push) but through a different route.

The advantage of our route is that it can handle the cases where natural law absolutism produces bizarre conclusions. Natural law holds that you must not lie to a murderer asking where your children are hiding, because lying directly attacks the basic good of knowledge. Most readers find this monstrous, and most contemporary natural law theorists find ways to mitigate it. But the mitigations always look like departures from the strict view. Our framework can simply say: in this case the override conditions are met, honesty is a strong default but not metaphysically absolute, and protecting the children is the right choice.

The framework’s response: the game-theoretic grounding of rules preserves the strength of natural law’s absolutes in normal cases while allowing principled deviation in extreme cases, without requiring the metaphysics that makes absolute prohibitions difficult to revise even when clearly wrong.

Disagreement 5: Moral Progress and the Fixed-Nature Problem

If natural law is fixed because human nature is fixed, then genuine moral progress is hard to explain. The abolition of slavery, the expansion of political rights to women, the recognition of children as distinct persons with interests of their own, the moral seriousness now given to animal suffering — these look like discoveries, as if we came to see something we previously could not see. But if the natural law has always been the same and was always available to rational reflection, why did rational reflection repeatedly fail to notice it?

Natural law theorists have responses. One is that the core principles were always there but the applications were obscured by sin, prejudice, or limited empirical knowledge — slavery was always wrong, but the error was protected by ideological fog and the difficulty of the application. Another is that there is less progress than appears; some past views were defensible in their context and the progress narrative oversimplifies. Both responses have merit.

But neither fully accommodates the framework’s Chapter 5 argument about the historical track record of moral blindness. That track record is long, systematic, and sobering. The most plausible explanation is not that each past generation was simply failing to apply unchanging principles, but that the moral circle expands as our understanding of who counts and why improves, and that this expansion is a real learning process, not merely the unveiling of pre-known truths. Our framework is built to expect such expansion and has architecture for handling it. Natural law, in its traditional form, is less well-equipped for this because its self-understanding treats the content as already given.

The framework’s response: moral epistemology is progressive and fallible, and our architecture should reflect this. Natural law’s commitment to fixed content creates friction with moral progress in a way that our framework does not.

Disagreement 6: The Common Good Problem

Both natural law and our framework invoke “the common good.” For Aquinas, the common good is the end of political community and the standard by which laws are evaluated. For us, the common good emerges from the game-theoretic analysis of coordination: arrangements that produce more flourishing and less suffering are better than arrangements that produce less.

The natural law conception, though, tends to treat the common good as a substantive good that authoritative reasoners can identify and direct the community toward. This creates a risk: those who claim knowledge of the common good gain a license to impose it on those who do not. Historical natural law practice has included, at various points, persecution of heretics, suppression of dissent, and imposition of specific religious practices — all justified on the grounds that the true common good required it.

Our framework, with its epistemic humility (Chapter 2) and error-correction primacy (Chapter 18), is more resistant to this pathology. The common good is something we are still discovering, and any claim to know it definitively should be viewed with suspicion, especially when the claim is used to override the voices of those affected. Natural law’s confidence that reason can read the common good from nature has sometimes been a cover for confidence that the reader’s own preferences are the common good. Our framework tries to build structural checks against this.

The Deepest Issue: Sources of Normativity

The disagreements above cluster around a single deeper question: where does normative authority come from?

Natural law answers: from the intelligible order of reality, which (on Thomistic versions) is the expression of divine reason, and which (on Finnis’s version) is recognized by practical reason reflecting on what is intelligibly valuable.

Our framework answers: from the objective reality of conscious experience (valence is real), plus the minimal axiom that suffering matters, plus the constraints imposed by the mathematics of coordination and the limits of our epistemic access to reality.

These are different answers, but not as different as they might appear. Both say that morality is not arbitrary. Both say that moral truths answer to something beyond individual preference. Both say that reason has a central role in moral knowledge. The disagreement is about the structure of the grounding: whether moral truths are features of an ordered cosmos with intrinsic purposes (natural law), or whether they emerge from the interaction of specific natural facts (conscious experience, game theory, cognitive limits) with minimal axioms we explicitly own (our framework).

The framework’s bet is that the second grounding is more honest about what we actually know, more robust against the metaphysical objections raised in the last four centuries, and more able to accommodate moral progress. Natural law’s bet is that the second grounding is too thin to sustain the moral seriousness the tradition wants to preserve — that without a telic, ordered cosmos, moral language loses its grip.

We are taking the bet.

What We Take From Natural Law

Despite the disagreements, the framework takes a great deal from natural law:

  1. The insistence that moral truths are objective — not merely subjective or conventional.
  2. The idea that flourishing is multidimensional — not reducible to hedonic tone.
  3. The integration of moral and political theory — moral standards apply to laws and institutions, not just to individual choices.
  4. The seriousness given to practical reason — reasoning about action is genuine reasoning, not the rationalization of prior preference.
  5. The suspicion of arbitrary will — neither divine nor human will can make something right if it is not.
  6. The notion of common good — there is a good of the community that cannot be reduced to aggregated individual preferences.
  7. The acknowledgment of strong moral defaults — some things must almost never be done, even for good reasons.

These are not trivial takeaways. Much of what is valuable in contemporary human rights discourse, in constitutional jurisprudence, and in moral philosophy’s treatment of dignity and inviolability comes from the natural law tradition. The framework’s political and legal philosophy owes more to this tradition than its explicit citations suggest.

What we do not take is the metaphysical framework that generates the specific content.
